topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Meet the author and the grandmother
topics.h: Think of the oldest person you have known all your life. Could you sketch them in words so well that a stranger would recognise them? Khushwant Singh did exactly that.
p: Khushwant Singh was an Indian writer, journalist and historian; 'The Portrait of a Lady' is his true pen-portrait of his own grandmother.
Form: a character sketch or memoir, told in the first person ('I'), moving through phases of the narrator's life.
Setting moves in stages: the village in Punjab, then the city house, then his years abroad and his return.
The grandmother is old, short, fat and slightly bent, with a face criss-crossed by wrinkles; she always dresses in spotless white.
The 'lady' of the title is not a fashionable woman but a simple, saintly old woman, which makes the title gently ironic.

ex.q: Identify the genre: A writer recalls, in his own voice, how his grandmother looked, how she lived and how their bond changed over twenty years.
st: The writer narrates in the first person about a real person.
The focus is on one person's looks, habits and character.
It follows the stages of the writer's own life.
ex.a: It is a memoir-style character sketch (a pen-portrait) in first-person narration.

topics.rl: Many Indian families keep an album of a dadi or nani in a white saree or dupatta. Writing a 'portrait' of such a person is a common CBSE descriptive task.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Not pretty, but beautiful
topics.h: Can someone with a face full of wrinkles still be called beautiful? The author says yes, and he uses a single picture of snowy mountains to prove it.
p: A portrait of the grandfather hung in the drawing room: big turban, loose clothes, long white beard; he looked at least a hundred years old.
The narrator finds it hard, almost absurd, to imagine his grandparents as young people who had once played as children.
Simile: the grandmother is compared to a winter landscape in the mountains, an expanse of white peace and contentment.
Key line in idea: she could never have been pretty, but she was always beautiful, because her beauty came from within: serenity and faith.
Pretty = pleasant-looking on the outside; beautiful here = a glow of goodness and calm from inside.

ex.q: Explain the simile: The grandmother is like a winter landscape in the mountains.
st: Find the two things compared: the grandmother and a snowy mountain scene.
Find the link: white clothes, calm stillness, purity.
State the effect: she seems serene, pure and at peace.
ex.a: The simile shows her white dress and calm, peaceful nature, like a still, snow-covered mountain scene.

topics.rl: When we see a calm sadhu, an old teacher or a grandmother at a Gurdwara langar, we often feel their peace. That inner calm is the 'beauty' Khushwant Singh means.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Village days: school at the temple
topics.h: Before Google Calendar, a grandmother's routine ran a child's whole day: bath, prayers, school, and a walk home feeding the village dogs.
p: The narrator's parents lived in the city, so as a child he lived in the village with his grandmother, who looked after him.
Each morning she woke him, bathed and dressed him, and sang her morning prayers in a sing-song voice, hoping he would learn them by heart.
She got his wooden slate, ink-pot and reed pen ready and walked with him to the village school, which was attached to the temple.
While the priest taught the children, she sat inside the temple reading the scriptures; then they walked home together.
On the way back they fed stale chapattis to the village dogs, which followed them and fought over the bread: a sign of her kindness to animals.

ex.q: Put her morning routine in order: walk to school, wake and bathe him, sing prayers while dressing him, read scriptures in the temple.
st: First she woke and bathed him.
She dressed him while singing her morning prayers.
She walked him to the temple school.
She read the scriptures while he studied.
ex.a: Wake and bathe him, dress him while singing prayers, walk to the temple school, read scriptures in the temple.

topics.rl: In many Indian villages the pathshala was once held in a temple or gurdwara courtyard. Even today, grandparents often walk young children to school and share leftover rotis with street dogs.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Move to the city and the English school
topics.h: Imagine your nani, who taught you shlokas, hearing that your new school teaches only science and English, with not a word about God. That was this grandmother's shock.
p: The parents settled in the city and sent for them; the narrator joined an English school and went there by motor bus.
She could not go with him to school, and she could not help with lessons in English, Western science or learning.
They still shared a room, but they saw less of each other; this was the turning-point in their friendship.
She disliked that he was taught about the law of gravity, Archimedes' principle and the world being round, and nothing about God or the scriptures.
Three reasons she was disturbed: she could not go with him; she could not help with his lessons; the school taught no God or scriptures (and later, music).

ex.q: Board-style question: Give three reasons why the grandmother was unhappy with the city school.
st: Reason 1: he went by motor bus, so she could no longer accompany him.
Reason 2: she could not help with lessons in English and Western science.
Reason 3: there was no teaching about God and the scriptures, and music was taught.
ex.a: She could not accompany him or help him, and she disliked the absence of religious teaching and the teaching of music.

topics.rl: Many families in India today discuss the same balance: coding classes and JEE coaching on one side, values and culture on the other. The grandmother stands for the old side of that debate.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: The music lesson and the sparrows
topics.h: One sentence, 'we are being given music lessons', made a gentle grandmother fall silent. Why would music upset anyone so much?
p: When he told her he was learning music, she was deeply disturbed; to her, music was not for gentlefolk but for harlots and beggars.
After this she rarely spoke to him: the music lesson deepened the break that had begun with the move to the city.
She found a new pastime: feeding sparrows in the courtyard of the city house with little bits of bread.
The sparrows came in hundreds, perched on her legs, shoulders and even her head, and she smiled and never shooed them away.
Three phases before he went abroad: close companions in the village; drifting apart in the city; separate lives once he went to university.

ex.q: Board question: Name the three phases of the author's relationship with his grandmother before he went abroad.
st: Phase 1 (village): constant companions; she took him to school.
Phase 2 (city): shared a room but drifted apart; music lesson made her silent.
Phase 3 (university): he got a room of his own; the link snapped.
ex.a: Village closeness, city drift, and separation once he had his own room at university.

topics.rl: Today music is a respected career in India, from Hindustani classical to film scores. The grandmother's view shows how attitudes in older generations could be very different.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: University, solitude and goodbye
topics.h: A goodbye at a railway station with no tears, no hug, just moving lips and prayer beads. Was she cold, or something deeper?
p: At university he was given a room of his own; the common link of their friendship snapped.
She accepted her loneliness quietly, with resignation: no complaints, no self-pity.
Her day: spinning at her spinning wheel from sunrise to sunset, saying prayers, and in the afternoon feeding the sparrows.
When he left to study abroad for five years, she came to the station but showed no emotion; her lips moved in prayer and her fingers told her beads.
She kissed his forehead; he treasured the moist mark as perhaps the last physical contact between them.

ex.q: Short answer: Mention three ways she spent her days after he grew up.
st: She sat at her spinning wheel from sunrise to sunset.
She recited prayers and told her beads.
In the afternoon she fed the sparrows.
ex.a: Spinning all day, praying with her beads, and feeding the sparrows in the afternoon.

topics.rl: Many elderly Indians live alone today while children work in Bengaluru, Dubai or Toronto. Like her, many fill their days with routine, prayer and small acts of care.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Homecoming and the drum
topics.h: A woman who never missed a prayer in her life spends one evening thumping an old drum and singing about warriors coming home. Then, for the first time, she forgets to pray.
p: After five years he returned; she received him at the station, clasped him in her arms, and her lips moved in prayer.
That evening a change came over her: she gathered the women of the neighbourhood, got an old, dilapidated drum and sang for hours of the homecoming of warriors.
The family had to persuade her to stop so that she would not overstrain herself.
That was the first time the narrator had known her not to pray: a hint that her end was near.
Next morning she had a mild fever; the doctor said it would pass, but she said her end had come and would not waste her last hours talking.

ex.q: Board question: What was unusual about the grandmother's behaviour just before her death?
st: She, who usually prayed, spent the evening singing and drumming with women.
She sang songs of warriors' homecoming for hours.
For the first time she missed her prayers, and next day she stopped talking to pray.
ex.a: She celebrated his return by drumming and singing for hours, missed her prayers for the first time, and then refused to talk so she could pray till the end.

topics.rl: In Punjab, a soldier or a family member returning home is still welcomed with dhol, songs and gidda. The grandmother's drum fits this tradition of joyful homecoming.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Her death and the silent sparrows
topics.h: Thousands of sparrows sit on a floor without a single chirp, ignoring the bread thrown to them. Nature itself seems to be mourning.
p: She lay peacefully in bed, praying and telling her beads, until her lips stopped moving and the rosary fell from her lifeless fingers.
As is customary, the family laid her on the floor, covered her with a red shroud, and left to arrange the funeral.
In the evening thousands of sparrows sat silently around her body in the room and verandah; there was no chirping.
The narrator's mother threw them bread crumbs, but they did not touch them; when the body was carried away, they flew away quietly.
Symbolism: the sparrows are silent mourners, returning her love; next morning the sweeper swept the uneaten crumbs away.

ex.q: Board question: How did the sparrows express their sorrow?
st: They gathered in thousands around her body.
They sat silently, without chirping.
They ignored the bread crumbs and flew away quietly only after the body was taken.
ex.a: They sat in silence around her body, ignored the bread, and flew away quietly once she was carried off.

topics.rl: Stories of animals mourning are not only literary: elephants in Assam and Kerala have been seen standing by a dead companion. The sparrow scene uses this bond to honour her kindness.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Character sketch of the grandmother
topics.h: Examiners love 'Write a character sketch of the grandmother'. The trick: one trait plus one proof from the story, every time.
p: Deeply religious: she prays all day, tells her beads constantly and reads the scriptures in the temple.
Affectionate and caring: she looks after the boy in every way in the village; strong-willed yet dignified in later life.
Compassionate to creatures: chapattis for the village dogs, bread for the sparrows.
Traditional: her values clash with Western education, science and music lessons.
Serene and self-reliant: she accepts loneliness without complaint and faces death calmly.

ex.q: Write the trait-proof pairs for 'religious' and 'compassionate'.
st: Religious: her lips always moved in prayer and she read scriptures at the temple.
Compassionate: she fed stale chapattis to dogs and bread to sparrows.
Link each trait with a clear incident.
ex.a: Religious: constant prayer and beads. Compassionate: feeding dogs and sparrows.

topics.rl: A good character sketch works like a cricket commentary with stats: each claim (trait) is backed by evidence (an incident).

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Themes: generations, ageing and nature
topics.h: Every generation thinks the next one has lost something. This story asks whether love can survive when two people stop sharing a world.
p: Changing relationship: love stays, but closeness fades as the boy grows and moves into a new world.
Ageing and loneliness: the old adapt to change with routine, faith and quiet acceptance.
Tradition versus modernity: temple school and scriptures versus English, science and music.
Humans and nature: her love for dogs and sparrows is returned when the sparrows mourn her.
Did their feelings change? Their closeness changed; their affection did not, as her joy at his return shows.

ex.q: Discussion: Did their feelings for each other change?
st: Look at the drift: city school, music lesson, separate room.
Look at the evidence of love: her joy at his return, the drum, his tender memory of her.
Conclude with a balanced view.
ex.a: Their closeness and shared world changed, but their love remained, as her celebration on his return shows.

topics.rl: Indian homes often have three generations under one roof. Grandparents may not understand a teen's coding projects, but the love shows in small acts, just like this story.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Style: humour, phases and words in context
topics.h: A memoir about death that still makes you smile? Khushwant Singh's light touch is part of why this text is so loved.
p: Gentle humour and irony: the idea of the grandparents being young, even playing children's games, seems absurd to the narrator.
Narration is chronological and in phases (village, city, university, abroad, return), told as first-person reminiscence.

Words in context: 'revolting' = disgusting/unbelievable; 'turning-point' = moment of decisive change; 'seclusion' = being alone; 'resignation' = calm acceptance; 'respite' = short rest; 'dilapidated' = old and falling apart.
'Tell' has many senses: tell beads = count them while praying; tell = inform; can't tell = can't be sure; tell apart = distinguish.

ex.q: Give the meaning of 'tell' in: (a) She told her beads. (b) I can't tell which twin is Riya.
st: (a) Beads are counted while praying, so 'tell' = count.
(b) Here 'tell' means to know or distinguish for sure.
ex.a: (a) count beads in prayer; (b) be sure / distinguish.

topics.rl: Indian cricket commentary often uses gentle humour to soften tense moments; Khushwant Singh does the same with sad memories.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Language lab: phrasal verbs, walking words and past perfect
topics.h: 'Hobbled', 'trudged', 'swaggered': one verb can show age, tiredness or pride. Good writers pick walking words like a bowler picks deliveries.
p: 'Take to' = begin as a habit (she took to feeding sparrows); 'take ill' = fall sick (she was taken ill).

Walking words: shuffle (drag feet), stride (long, confident steps), waddle (sway like a duck), swagger (proud, showy walk), trudge (slow, tired steps), slink (move quietly, guiltily), hobble (limp, walk with difficulty), lumber (move heavily, clumsily).
Past perfect (had + past participle) shows an action completed before another past action: 'She had lived in the village before they moved.'
The narrator would have spoken Punjabi with his grandmother; 'a dilapidated drum' could be rendered in Hindi as 'tooti-phooti dholak'.
Writing task: a short descriptive portrait of someone you were fond of, using appearance, habits, an incident and your feelings.

ex.q: Correct the tense: 'When we reached the station, the train left already.'
st: Two past actions: we reached; the train left.
The leaving happened first, so it takes the past perfect.
Use 'had left'.
ex.a: When we reached the station, the train had already left.

topics.rl: On Indian Railways announcements and in news reports you hear the past perfect all the time: 'The train had already departed when the passengers arrived.'

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Portrait of a Lady
topics.t: Exam practice: answers that score
topics.h: Short answers in 40–50 words, extract MCQs, and one long answer. Here is how to get full marks on 'The Portrait of a Lady'.
p: Short answer (40–50 words): answer the exact question, give one or two text details, no story retelling.
Extract MCQs: read the lines, then answer on meaning, tone, device or inference using clues in the extract itself.
Long answer (120–150 words): plan intro, three body points with incidents, and a conclusion linking to the theme.
Typical long answers: the grandmother as a symbol of the older generation; the changing relationship; her strength of character.
Use your own words; quote only a few words if needed.

ex.q: Paraphrased extract: The old lady limped about the house in spotless white, one hand on her waist to support her bent back, the other counting rosary beads. What traits are suggested?
st: 'Limped' and 'bent back' suggest old age and frailty.
Counting rosary beads suggests religious devotion.
'Spotless white' suggests purity and simplicity.
ex.a: She is old and frail, yet devout and pure in her ways.

topics.rl: Board toppers in CBSE English often say the same thing: plan for one minute, then write. A clear structure earns more than a long retelling.

topics.t: The poet and the seaside snapshot
topics.h: Scroll back far enough in a family album and you find someone you love, as a child you never knew. Shirley Toulson's poem begins with exactly such a picture.
p: Shirley Toulson was a British poet and writer; 'A Photograph' reflects on an old photo of her late mother.
Form: three stanzas of free verse with no regular rhyme scheme; each stanza is a different time phase.
Stanza 1: a mounted cardboard photograph shows her mother at about twelve on a seaside holiday, paddling in the sea.
Her mother, the 'big girl', stands between her two younger cousins, Betty and Dolly, each holding one of her hands.
Their uncle took the picture; the three girls stood still and smiled at him through their windblown hair.

ex.q: Describe the photograph in Stanza 1 in one sentence.
st: Who is in it: the mother and her cousins Betty and Dolly.
Where: paddling at the seaside.
Who took it: their uncle with the camera.
ex.a: It shows the poet's mother, about twelve, paddling in the sea with her cousins Betty and Dolly, smiling at their uncle who held the camera.

topics.rl: Before phones, a family trip to Juhu, Marina or Puri beach might produce just one or two prints, carefully pasted on cardboard. Those few pictures became treasured memories.

topics.t: Why 'cardboard'? Words in the poem
topics.h: The poem doesn't say 'the photograph shows me'. It says 'the cardboard shows me'. One odd word choice carries a whole mood.
p: 'Cardboard' denotes the stiff card on which old photographs were mounted; it also hints that the moment is now frozen and lifeless.
The camera captured a single happy moment: the three girls paddling and smiling, a moment that can never be lived again.
Paddling = walking or wading in shallow water.
Transient = lasting only a short time; wry = showing grim or dry amusement, often mixed with sadness.
Laboured = done with effort, not natural; circumstance = a fact or event, here the mother's death.

ex.q: Why does the poet use the word 'cardboard' instead of 'photograph'?
st: Literal meaning: old photos were pasted on cardboard mounts.
Suggested meaning: the image is stiff, frozen and without life.
Link: the living girl is gone; only a flat picture remains.
ex.a: Cardboard refers to the old mounted photo and suggests a frozen, lifeless record of a living moment.

topics.rl: Grandparents' wedding photos in many Indian homes are still pasted on stiff card frames. The card has lasted longer than the moment it holds.

topics.t: Stanza 2: the sea and the mother's laughter
topics.h: The sea in a photo looks the same today. The girls in it have grown up, grown old and gone. That contrast is the heart of Stanza 2.
p: The sea appears to have changed less than the people; it washed their short-lived ('transient') feet.
Twenty or thirty years later, the mother would laugh at the snapshot, pointing out Betty and Dolly and the old-fashioned way they were dressed for the beach.
The sea holiday was the mother's past; the mother's laughter is now the poet's past.
What has not changed: the sea. This suggests nature is lasting while human life passes quickly.
The mother's laugh shows fond nostalgia for her childhood, tinged with a sense of loss.

ex.q: What has not changed over the years, and what does that suggest?
st: The girls grew old; the mother is now dead.
The sea looks almost the same.
So nature is permanent, human life is short.
ex.a: The sea has not changed, suggesting the permanence of nature against the transience of human life.

topics.rl: Kanyakumari's waves have looked the same for centuries, while generations of visitors have come and gone. Toulson uses that same contrast.

topics.t: Bittersweet loss and the silence of death
topics.h: Some grief makes you cry. Some grief leaves you with no words at all. The last stanza of 'A Photograph' is about the second kind.
p: 'Both wry with the laboured ease of loss': mother and poet both look back with a bittersweet smile; the ease is forced, because loss lies underneath.
For the mother, the loss is her childhood; for the poet, the loss is her mother and her mother's laughter.
Stanza 3: the mother has now been dead for nearly as many years as the girl in the photo had lived (about twelve).
'This circumstance' is the mother's death; the poet says there is nothing at all to say about it.
'Its silence silences': the silence of death leaves the poet speechless; grief is too deep for words.

ex.q: Explain 'Its silence silences.'
st: 'Its' refers to the circumstance: the mother's death.
Death brings a silence: no more laughter or voice.
That silence makes the poet silent too; she cannot express her grief.
ex.a: The silence of her mother's death is so heavy that it leaves the poet herself speechless.

topics.rl: At an Indian chautha or shraddh, relatives often sit quietly near a photo garlanded with marigolds. The silence in that room says what words cannot.

topics.t: Themes and the three phases
topics.h: One photo, three time zones: a girl at the sea, a woman laughing at the girl, a daughter grieving for the woman. That's the structure examiners love to ask about.
p: Memory and nostalgia: a photograph triggers memories for two generations.
Passage of time: humans are transient; the sea is permanent.
Death, loss and grief: the loss of childhood, then the loss of a mother.
Three phases: Stanza 1 – the mother as a girl of twelve; Stanza 2 – the mother, twenty or thirty years later, laughing at the photo; Stanza 3 – the poet after the mother's death.
'This circumstance' (Stanza 3) refers to the mother's death.

ex.q: Board question: What are the three phases in the three stanzas?
st: Stanza 1: the photo at the seaside, the mother aged about twelve.
Stanza 2: the grown mother laughing at the photo.
Stanza 3: the poet remembering after the mother's death.
ex.a: Childhood at the beach; the mother's adult nostalgia; the poet's grief after her death.

topics.rl: Family WhatsApp groups often share an old black-and-white photo on a death anniversary. Memory, time and loss: the same three themes.

topics.t: Devices and exam practice
topics.h: Extract-based MCQs on this poem almost always test one of four things: contrast, oxymoron, the silence line, or the role of the photograph.
p: Contrast: changing human faces versus the unchanging sea.
Oxymoron: 'laboured ease' joins two opposite ideas (effort and ease).
'Its silence silences': repetition and personification; silence is shown acting on the poet. It is also read as a paradox.
Alliteration: 'terribly transient' (repeated 't'); vivid visual imagery of the girls paddling and smiling through their hair.
The photograph's role: it links the mother's childhood, her adult memories and the poet's present grief, making the poet face time and loss.

ex.q: Identify the device: 'the laboured ease of loss'.
st: 'Laboured' means with effort.
'Ease' means without effort.
Two opposite words placed together form an oxymoron.
ex.a: Oxymoron: 'laboured ease' combines opposites to show a forced calm.

topics.rl: Ad slogans use oxymorons too, like 'seriously funny' or 'deafening silence'. Poets use them to pack complex feelings into two words.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Setting sail: the dream voyage
topics.h: A family of four leaves England to sail around the world, retracing a voyage made two centuries earlier. What could go wrong? Almost everything.
p: A true survival account written by Gordon Cook and Alan East, narrated in the first person by the father, who is the ship's captain.
The text falls into three sections: the voyage and the first great wave; the fight to keep afloat; the search for and sighting of the island.
In July 1976 the narrator, his wife Mary, son Jonathan (6) and daughter Suzanne (7) set sail from Plymouth, England.
Their aim: to repeat the round-the-world voyage made 200 years earlier by Captain James Cook.
Their boat, Wavewalker, was a 23-metre, 30-ton wooden-hulled ship, professionally built, fitted out over months and tested in rough weather.

ex.q: Fill in the voyage card: start date, port, aim, ship.
st: Start: July 1976.
Port: Plymouth, England.
Aim: to retrace Captain James Cook's round-the-world voyage.
Ship: Wavewalker, 23 m long, 30 tons, wooden hull.
ex.a: July 1976, Plymouth; retrace Captain Cook's voyage; aboard the 23-metre, 30-ton Wavewalker.

topics.rl: Indian Navy officers Dilip Donde and Abhilash Tomy sailed solo around the world, and the INSV Tarini crew of women officers did it too. Long voyages need the same careful preparation as Wavewalker.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Into the southern Indian Ocean: precautions
topics.h: When waves start rising like mountains, a good captain doesn't panic. He runs a checklist. This section is that checklist.
p: At Cape Town two crewmen joined them, American Larry Vigil and Swiss Herb Seigler, to help on one of the world's roughest seas, the southern Indian Ocean.
They celebrated Christmas about 3,500 km east of Cape Town, despite the bad weather.
On 2 January the waves grew gigantic and the wind howled.
Precautions: they slowed the ship by dropping the storm jib, lashed a heavy mooring rope in a loop across the stern, and double-lashed everything on deck.
They went through their life-raft drill, attached life-lines, and put on oilskins and life jackets.

ex.q: List the steps the captain took to protect Wavewalker from the storm.
st: Slow the ship: drop the storm jib.
Steady her: lash a heavy mooring rope in a loop across the stern.
Secure everything: double-lash all items; practise the life-raft drill.
Protect people: life-lines, oilskins and life jackets.
ex.a: He dropped the storm jib, looped a mooring rope across the stern, double-lashed everything, ran the life-raft drill and had everyone wear life-lines, oilskins and life jackets.

topics.rl: Before a cyclone, Indian fishermen in Odisha and Andhra pull boats ashore and tie them down, following IMD warnings. Preparation saves lives, as on Wavewalker.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: The great wave and the flooded ship
topics.h: One wave, almost twice the height of the others, picks up a 30-ton ship. The captain is thrown into the sea, and only a life-line pulls him back.
p: On 2 January an enormous wave struck; the narrator's head hit the wheel and he was swept overboard.
The ship righted itself; his life-line jerked tight and he grabbed the guard rails and got back on board.
His injuries: cracked ribs and a mouth full of blood and broken teeth. Mary took the wheel and held the ship steady.
Water poured in through a broken hatch and a gaping hole; the ship was listing and taking in water fast.
Larry and Herb pumped for hours; the narrator stretched canvas and fixed waterproof hatch covers across the holes, so most water was deflected over the side.

ex.q: How did the narrator stop water from pouring in?
st: Find what is broken: the hatch and a gaping hole.
Cover the gaps with canvas and waterproof hatch covers.
Result: most water now ran off over the side.
ex.a: He stretched canvas and fixed waterproof hatch covers over the gaps, so most water was deflected over the side.

topics.rl: Coast Guard and NDRF teams in Kerala's 2018 floods also worked on two fronts at once: stop water coming in, and get water out. The Wavewalker crew did both.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Pumps, a brave daughter and a tiny island
topics.h: When your seven-year-old hides a head injury so as not to distract you, and your six-year-old says he's not afraid to die if the family is together, you fight harder.
p: Problems: the hand pumps blocked with debris and the electric pump short-circuited.
Solution: the narrator found another electric pump, connected it to an outlet pipe, and it worked.
Sue had a huge bump on her head, two black eyes and a deep cut on her arm, but did not complain because she did not want to worry her father.
Jonathan told his father that they were not afraid of dying if they could all be together, which gave the title.
With little equipment, the narrator worked out their position and set a course for Ile Amsterdam, a tiny island, a pinprick in the vast ocean.

ex.q: Why did Sue hide her injury?
st: She had a bump on her head, black eyes and a cut arm.
Her father was busy trying to save the ship.
She did not want to worry him or distract him.
ex.a: She did not want to worry her father while he was trying to save everyone.

topics.rl: Children often show surprising calm in crises; during the Chennai floods many kids helped neighbours stay cheerful. Sue and Jonathan show the same courage.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Land ho! The final days
topics.h: After days of pumping, a kid's hand-drawn card and a hug decide the mood on board. Then two small voices shout that they can see land.
p: 4 January: after about 36 hours of pumping, the water was under control; they ate their first proper meal in almost two days, and felt relieved.
The relief was short-lived: the wind rose again, and by 5 January the situation was desperate.
Sue gave her parents a card with caricatures of them, telling them how much she loved them and thanking them.
Jonathan hugged his father and called him the best daddy and the best captain in the world.
On 6 January, in the evening, the children spotted Ile Amsterdam; the people at the island's French scientific base helped them ashore.

ex.q: Board question: Describe the mental condition of the voyagers on 4 and 5 January.
st: 4 January: pumping succeeded; they ate and felt relief and hope.
Then the wind returned.
5 January: the situation was desperate; they feared for their lives but kept spirits up.
ex.a: On 4 January they felt relief and hope; on 5 January they were full of fear and near despair, yet the children's love kept them going.

topics.rl: The Indian Coast Guard and Navy run search-and-rescue across a huge area of the Indian Ocean. A sighting of land or a rescue ship after days at sea still brings the same 'Land ho!' joy.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Characters and the three-part narrative
topics.h: Adults panic about what could happen; children trust whoever is in charge. In this crisis, the kids end up as the steadiest people on board.
p: The narrator: calm, resourceful and determined captain; also a loving father who feels responsible for everyone.
Mary: brave and steady; she held the wheel through the most crucial hours and supported the family.
Larry and Herb: tireless crewmen who pumped for hours and never gave up.
Sue and Jonathan: show remarkable maturity, courage and optimism; adults feel fear more openly, children show trust and love.

Narration shifts: Section 1 – an adventurous voyage turning into crisis; Section 2 – desperate struggle to survive; Section 3 – hope, relief and rescue. Possible subtitles: 'The Voyage Begins', 'Fighting to Stay Afloat', 'Land Ho!'

ex.q: Give suitable subtitles to the three sections.
st: Section 1 tells of the start and the great wave.
Section 2 is the struggle with water and pumps.
Section 3 is the search for and sighting of the island.
ex.a: 1: 'The Voyage and the Wave'; 2: 'Fighting to Stay Afloat'; 3: 'Land Ho!'

topics.rl: Indian Railways' accident relief teams depend on every member: driver, guard, medic. Wavewalker's survival also depended on each person doing a part.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Themes: courage, teamwork, nature
topics.h: Why would anyone choose to sail into the world's roughest ocean? And what do you learn when you almost don't come back?
p: Courage and optimism: the family keeps hope alive under extreme stress.
Teamwork, family bonding and leadership: everyone has a job, and the captain leads calmly.
Human endurance against nature's fury: the ocean is huge and powerful, but persistence wins.
Why people take hazardous voyages: the thrill of adventure, testing one's limits, discovery, and a chance to see life's essentials clearly.
Lessons from facing death: love, unity and optimism matter most; panic helps no one.

ex.q: Discussion: What lessons can one learn from facing death in this account?
st: Optimism kept them working even when things looked hopeless.
Teamwork and family unity mattered more than anything else.
Calm leadership and careful planning saved them.
ex.a: Hope, unity and calm thinking matter most when life is at stake.

topics.rl: Mountaineers like Bachendri Pal and Arunima Sinha talk about the same reasons for risky journeys: testing oneself, and coming back with a clearer view of life.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Sea words: from stern to starboard
topics.h: Stern, jib, hatch, starboard: if sailing words sound like a foreign language, this topic is your phrasebook.
p: Expressions: 'honing our seafaring skills' = sharpening sailing skills; 'ominous silence' = a threatening quiet; 'Mayday calls' = international radio distress calls; 'pinpricks in the vast ocean' = tiny islands; 'a tousled head' = messy, untidy hair.

Ship parts: bow = front; stern = back; port = left side and starboard = right side (facing forward); deck = floor on top; hull = body of the ship; hatch = opening in the deck; jib = triangular front sail.

Everyday meanings: knot (unit of ship speed / a tied loop), stern (strict / back of a ship), boom (sudden growth / sail pole), hatch (to come out of an egg / deck opening), anchor (TV presenter / weight that holds a ship).
Ship compounds: airship (powered balloon), flagship (lead ship, or best product of a company), lightship (anchored ship with a light that works as a lighthouse).
'Take on': here 'take on water' = let water in; also take on staff (employ), take on a job (accept), take on a rival (compete with).

ex.q: What does 'take on' mean in: (a) The ship took on water. (b) The firm took on ten engineers.
st: (a) Water came into the ship.
(b) The firm employed them.
ex.a: (a) let in water; (b) employed.

topics.rl: Mumbai and Visakhapatnam port pilots speak this language daily. And business news calls Tata's or Infosys's top product its 'flagship'.

topics.ch: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together
topics.t: Language links and exam practice
topics.h: The English word 'catamaran' sailed in from Tamil. Indian boat words and boatmen's songs are part of the same story of the sea.
p: 'Catamaran' comes from Tamil 'kattumaram', meaning 'tied wood': logs tied together to make a boat.
Indian languages have many words for storm, such as toofan and aandhi in Hindi; and many vessel names such as dhow, dinghy, kayak, canoe, junk and catamaran.
India has rich boatmen's songs, like the bhatiyali of Bengal and the vanchipattu of Kerala.
Short answers (40–50 words) on events and characters; long answer (120–150 words) on courage and optimism; extract MCQs on lines and words.

ex.q: Long answer plan: 'Optimism helps us survive the most difficult situations.' Use the text.
st: Intro: the family's crisis in the southern Indian Ocean.
Body 1: the captain keeps working and navigating.
Body 2: the children's words and card lift morale.
Body 3: teamwork keeps the ship afloat; they reach Ile Amsterdam.
Conclusion: hope turned despair into survival.
ex.a: A structured answer: intro, three evidence-based points, conclusion linking optimism to survival.

topics.rl: Kerala's snake-boat races during Onam are accompanied by vanchipattu boat songs. Every coast has its own sea vocabulary and music.

topics.ch: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues
topics.t: Who was Tut? The mystery begins
topics.h: A teenage king dies about 3,300 years ago, and the world is still asking how. This ancient cold case was reopened with a hospital scanner.
p: 'Discovering Tut: the Saga Continues' is a non-fiction feature by A.R. Williams, written for National Geographic, on the CT scan of Tutankhamun's mummy.
It blends archaeology, history and modern forensic science to explore an ancient mystery.
Tutankhamun (Tut) was a teenage pharaoh who died about 3,300 years ago, at around nineteen.
He was the last heir of a powerful family that had ruled Egypt and its empire for centuries.
His early death is a mystery: was it illness, an accident, or murder? Scientists hoped scans would give clues.

ex.q: Classify the text: It reports the CT scan of a real mummy, explains history and quotes experts.
st: It deals with real people and events.
It reports facts and expert opinions.
It was written for a science and geography magazine.
ex.a: It is a non-fiction feature article (science and history journalism).

topics.rl: AIIMS forensic experts use scans and evidence to answer questions about causes of death. Egyptologists did the same with Tut, just 33 centuries late.

topics.ch: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues
topics.t: Tut's family: from Aten back to Amun
topics.h: Imagine a ruler who shuts down the main temples, smashes images and builds a brand-new capital for one god. Then his successor changes his own name to undo it all.
p: Amenhotep III, a powerful pharaoh who was Tut's father or grandfather, ruled for almost forty years.
His son Amenhotep IV took the name Akhenaten and promoted worship of the Aten, the sun disc.
Akhenaten attacked the god Amun, closed his temples, and moved the religious capital from Thebes to a new city, Akhetaten (now called Amarna). Egyptologist Ray Johnson called him 'wacky'.
After a short-lived ruler, Smenkhkare, the young Tutankhaten took the throne.
He changed his name to Tutankhamun ('living image of Amun') and restored the old worship of Amun.

ex.q: Why did Tut change his name?
st: His birth name Tutankhaten honoured the Aten.
As king he restored worship of Amun.
So he took the name Tutankhamun, 'living image of Amun'.
ex.a: He changed it to honour Amun, whose worship he restored after Akhenaten's changes.

topics.rl: Rulers changing names or capitals is a recurring pattern in history; Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, a move often studied in Indian history class.

topics.ch: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues
topics.t: 1922: Howard Carter opens the tomb
topics.h: Gold coffins, a gold mask, chariots, games and even a razor for the afterlife, and a mummy glued in place by hardened resin. Carter's find was dazzling and messy.
p: The British archaeologist Howard Carter discovered Tut's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922.
Treasures: gilded coffins, a gold mask, chariots, weapons, furniture, jewellery, board games, linen, a bronze razor, and food and wine for the afterlife.
Ritual resins poured over the body had hardened and cemented the mummy to the bottom of its solid gold coffin.
Carter set it in the blazing sun for hours to loosen the resins, but this failed.
His men chiselled away the resin, removed the head and cut through nearly every major joint to free the body; it was reassembled on a bed of sand in a wooden box.

ex.q: Why did Carter's team chisel away the resins?
st: The resins had hardened like cement.
The mummy was stuck to the gold coffin.
Sunlight had failed to soften them, so they cut them away to free the body.
ex.a: Because the hardened resins had glued the mummy to the coffin and the sun had not loosened them.

topics.rl: When the ASI excavates sites like Keeladi or Rakhigarhi today, it uses careful layer-by-layer methods precisely so that remains are not damaged as in early digs.

topics.ch: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues
topics.t: Carter's legacy and the 1968 X-ray
topics.h: Today, archaeologists respect remains as people. By that standard, Carter's 1920s methods look harsh, and the mummy has been examined again and again ever since.
p: Carter's methods are resented today as crude and treasure-focused; they showed little respect for Tut as a person.
Carter argued that robbers would otherwise have stripped the body of its gold.
In 1968, more than forty years after the discovery, an anatomy professor X-rayed the mummy and found that its breastbone and front ribs were missing.
Tut's body has been examined repeatedly because each new technology (X-ray, then CT) promised fresh answers about his life and death.
Reasons often asked: why the body was studied repeatedly, why Carter is resented, why he chiselled the resins, why treasures were buried, why Tut changed his name.

ex.q: Give a reason: Why is Carter's investigation resented today?
st: His men cut the body apart.
His focus was on gold and treasure.
Modern ethics demand respect for the dead.
ex.a: Because his crude methods damaged the body and showed more interest in treasure than in respect for Tut.

topics.rl: India's museums now follow guidelines on handling human remains with dignity. Ethics in science, like in medicine at AIIMS, is a growing concern worldwide.

topics.ch: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues
topics.t: The 2005 CT scan
topics.h: A desert night, howling wind, dust devils, and a hospital-grade scanner parked in a trailer outside a 3,300-year-old tomb. Then the machine stops.
p: On 5 January 2005, Zahi Hawass, Secretary General of Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities, oversaw the CT scanning of Tut's mummy.
A portable CT scanner sat in a trailer near the tomb; the night was windy, with 'dust devils' and dark-bellied clouds moving across the sky.
The scanner briefly failed when sand clogged a cooling fan; substitute fans let the work continue.
CT (computed tomography) took about 1,700 cross-section X-ray images, which build a 3-D virtual body.

Aim: to settle questions about his death and age. Tut became one of the first mummies to be CT-scanned, 'first' in death as he was in life. The scan revealed his remains in eerie detail, and the mummy was returned to his tomb.

ex.q: Why is Tut called 'first' in death as in life?
st: In life he was king, first among his people.
In death he was among the first mummies to be CT-scanned.
So he leads the way in both.
ex.a: As king he was first in life, and as one of the first mummies scanned he leads in death too.

topics.rl: Indian hospitals run CT scanners round the clock; a typical scan stacks thin X-ray slices into a 3-D picture, the same principle used on Tut.

topics.ch: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues
topics.t: Science, respect and the curse
topics.h: Should we scan the dead, or leave them in peace? The Tut story sits right on that line between curiosity and respect.
p: Science and technology help solve historical mysteries: X-rays, CT scans and DNA give evidence instead of guesses.
Respect for the dead and their rituals must be balanced with scientific curiosity.
Ancient Egyptians believed in an afterlife, so royalty were buried with treasures and daily objects for the journey.
Myths like the 'pharaoh's curse' claim bad luck follows anyone who disturbs a tomb; evidence-based science does not support such superstition.
Debate points: scientific study can give conclusive evidence and add to knowledge, but it should respect cultural and religious traditions.

ex.q: Debate: Is scientific study of ancient remains justified?
st: For: it gives evidence, solves mysteries and helps us understand the past.
Against: it may disturb the dead and hurt cultural feelings.
Balanced view: allow research with respect and careful methods.
ex.a: Yes, if done respectfully, non-invasively and with care for cultural traditions.

topics.rl: ISRO's Chandrayaan used science to answer questions people once settled with myths. Science asks for evidence, while respecting what places mean to people.

topics.ch: Hornbill: Discovering Tut: The Saga Continues
topics.t: Word study, medical terms and exam practice
topics.h: CT, MRI, ECG, biopsy: hospital words you've heard on TV. This lesson turns them, and some lovely phrases, into exam marks.
p: Phrases: forensic reconstruction (rebuilding a face or body from evidence); scudded across (moved fast); casket grey (dull grey like a coffin); resurrection (coming back to life); funerary treasures (objects buried with the dead); circumvented (got around); eerie detail (strangely clear detail).
Collocations: ghostly dust devils, desert sky, stunning artefacts, scientific detachment, eternal brilliance, ritual resins, virtual body.

Medical terms: CT scan (cross-section X-rays), MRI (magnets and radio waves), autopsy or post-mortem (examination after death), dialysis (cleaning blood when kidneys fail), ECG (records heart's electrical activity), angiography (X-ray of blood vessels with dye), biopsy (tissue sample for testing).
Languages become extinct when speakers shift to dominant languages; they can be saved by teaching children, recording them and using them in media.
Exam focus: short answers on Carter, the CT scan and Tut's lineage; long answer on science versus tradition.

ex.q: Match the test: A doctor takes a small piece of tissue to check for disease. Name it.
st: A tissue sample is removed.
It is examined under a microscope.
This is called a biopsy.
ex.a: Biopsy.

topics.rl: UNESCO lists many Indian languages as endangered, and the Central Institute of Indian Languages in Mysuru documents them. Recording a grandparent's language is real preservation work.

topics.t: Ted Hughes and the silent tree
topics.h: A tree in September sun: no wind, no birds, a few yellow leaves. It looks like nothing is happening. Ted Hughes is about to prove otherwise.
p: Ted Hughes was a British poet, Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom, famous for vivid poems about nature and animals.
'The Laburnum Top' is a short descriptive nature poem in free verse about a goldfinch visiting a laburnum tree.
Opening: the top of the laburnum is silent and quite still in the yellow afternoon sunlight of September; a few leaves are yellowing and all its seeds have fallen.
Laburnum: a tree with hanging yellow flowers. In India, the similar amaltas is called the 'Indian laburnum' (golden shower tree).

Key words: goldfinch (small finch with gold-yellow wing bars), startlement (sudden surprise), chitterings (twittering sounds), sleek (smooth and glossy), eerie (strange), subsides (sinks back, settles down).

ex.q: What mood does the opening create?
st: Silent, still tree.
Late, quiet September afternoon.
Leaves yellowing, seeds fallen: the season is ending.
ex.a: A calm, lifeless, slightly sleepy mood: nature at rest, waiting.

topics.rl: In April–May, amaltas trees across Delhi, Kerala and Maharashtra burst into hanging yellow flowers. Kerala's state flower, kanikonna, is this tree.

topics.t: Enter the goldfinch: sleek as a lizard
topics.h: Have you ever seen a lizard on a wall freeze, then dart? Ted Hughes says the goldfinch moves exactly like that.
p: The goldfinch arrives suddenly with a twitching chirrup: a suddenness, a startlement at a branch end.
Simile: she is 'sleek as a lizard', alert and abrupt.
Why a lizard? Like a lizard, she is smooth, watchful and moves in quick, sudden darts, not in a smooth glide.
Her arrival breaks the silence and stillness of the tree.
The goldfinch is female ('she'), a mother returning to her nest.

ex.q: Explain why the bird's movement is compared to a lizard's.
st: Lizards are sleek, alert and move in sudden darts.
The goldfinch enters the tree quickly and watchfully.
The comparison shows her speed, caution and alertness.
ex.a: Like a lizard, she is sleek, alert and abrupt, darting quickly and cautiously into the tree.

topics.rl: Watch a house gecko on a Mumbai balcony wall: still, still, then a sudden dash. That is the motion Hughes gives the bird.

topics.t: The tree becomes an engine
topics.h: A silent tree suddenly hums with chirps and trembling wings, like a machine switched on. Hughes calls it 'the engine of her family'.
p: She enters the thick leaves where her nest of chicks is hidden; a machine of chitterings, trillings and trembling wings starts up.
Metaphor: the whole tree trembles and thrills; it is 'the engine of her family'.
She 'stokes' it full: like a stoker feeding an engine, she feeds the chicks and they burst into sound.
Then she flirts out (moves quickly and lightly) to a branch end, showing her 'barred face identity mask'.
The barred face: the goldfinch's striped red, white and black face markings, like a mask by which she is identified.

ex.q: Why is the image of an engine used?
st: Before she comes, the tree is still, like a switched-off engine.
Her arrival sets off noise and vibration: chirps, trills, trembling.
She 'stokes' it, feeding the chicks as a stoker fuels an engine.
ex.a: Because the chicks' noise and movement make the tree throb with life, like an engine she starts up and fuels.

topics.rl: An auto-rickshaw sitting silent, then sputtering to life when started: that switch from still to buzzing is the engine image in the poem.

topics.t: She launches away: the circle closes
topics.h: Silence, then life, then silence again. The poem ends exactly where it began, but now we know what the silence was waiting for.
p: With an eerie, delicate whistle-chirrup, the goldfinch launches away 'towards the infinite' (the vast open sky).
The laburnum subsides to empty: silent and still again, as at the start.
Circular structure: the poem begins and ends with silence and stillness; life comes in the middle.
Onomatopoeia: chirrup, chitterings, trillings, whistle-chirrup, words that imitate the sounds they name.
How the poem begins and ends: it begins with a still, silent tree and ends with the tree empty and calm again after the bird leaves.

ex.q: How does the poem begin and end?
st: Beginning: silent, still laburnum in September sun.
Middle: the bird brings noise and movement.
End: the bird leaves and the tree subsides to empty.
ex.a: It begins and ends in silence and stillness, with a burst of life in between: a circular structure.

topics.rl: An Indian Railways platform at 3 a.m. is silent, roars to life when a train arrives, and goes quiet again when it leaves: the same circle.

topics.t: Themes and the music of the poem
topics.h: Behind one small bird visiting one tree, Hughes hides three big ideas: silence versus life, the cycle of life, and how nature depends on itself.
p: Contrast: silence and stillness versus sound and movement.
Cycle of life: life arrives, energises the tree and departs; motherhood and family care are at the centre.
Interdependence: the tree shelters the bird's family; the birds bring the tree to life.
Alliteration: 'trembles and thrills', 'a suddenness, a startlement'; imagery: visual (yellow September sunlight, barred face) and auditory (chirrup, trillings).

Personification: the tree 'trembles and thrills' and 'subsides' as if it had feelings. Local connections: laburnum is like the amaltas; a local bird to compare could be any small songbird you see, such as a sunbird or bulbul.

ex.q: Identify the alliteration and its effect: 'The whole tree trembles and thrills.'
st: Repeated sounds: 'tr' in tree, trembles, and 'th' in thrills.
The repeated consonants copy the quivering movement.
Effect: we almost hear and feel the tree vibrating.
ex.a: Alliteration of t/tr sounds makes the tree's excited quivering vivid.

topics.rl: A mango tree in an Indian courtyard is shelter for koels, mynas and squirrels; take the birds away and the tree feels silent. That is the poem's interdependence.

topics.t: Exam practice: extracts and favourite lines
topics.h: Extract MCQs on this poem test four things again and again: the lizard, the engine, the mask and the circle. Nail those and you're set.
p: Extract MCQs: identify the device (simile, metaphor, onomatopoeia, alliteration), meaning of a word, or the mood.
Short answer: describe the relationship between the tree and the bird (shelter, life, family).
Personal response: pick a part you like and justify with a device and its effect.
Keep quotes to a few words; explain in your own words.

ex.q: Personal response: Which part of the poem do you like most and why?
st: Choose a part: e.g., the engine image.
Say what it means: the chicks make the tree throb with life.
Say why you like it: it turns a quiet tree into a busy machine, a surprising and vivid picture.
ex.a: The engine image, because it makes the silent tree suddenly pulse with life in a fresh, surprising way.

topics.rl: CBSE extract questions usually give 4–6 lines and ask 3–5 MCQs. A quick device checklist (simile, metaphor, alliteration, onomatopoeia, personification) saves time.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)
topics.t: Whitman asks the rain, 'Who are you?'
topics.h: What if you asked the monsoon who it was, and it answered? Walt Whitman's poem is exactly that conversation.
p: Walt Whitman was an American poet, often called the father of free verse; his famous collection is 'Leaves of Grass'.
'The Voice of the Rain' is a dialogue poem: the poet asks the soft-falling shower who it is, and the rain replies.
The poet asks, in old-fashioned words, 'And who art thou?' and the rain answers that it is the Poem of Earth.
Two voices: the poet (the opening question and the bracketed lines at the end) and the rain (the long answer in between).
'As here translated': the poet claims to translate the rain's answer into human words.

ex.q: Identify the two voices in the poem.
st: The poet speaks first, asking the shower who it is.
The rain replies, describing itself as the Poem of Earth and its journey.
The bracketed lines at the end are the poet's comment.
ex.a: The poet (question and bracketed lines) and the rain (the reply in between).

topics.rl: Every June, Kerala welcomes the monsoon as if it were a guest. Whitman goes one step further and lets the rain introduce itself.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)
topics.t: The water cycle in verse
topics.h: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation: you learnt them in Class 6 science. Whitman puts the same cycle into the rain's own mouth.
p: The rain rises unseen ('impalpable', not able to be touched) from the land and the bottomless sea, upward to the sky: evaporation.
In the sky it is vaguely formed, altogether changed, and yet the same: condensation into clouds.
It descends to wash ('lave') the droughts, the tiny particles ('atomies') and the dust-layers of the globe: precipitation.
The cycle repeats: water rises, changes form, falls and returns to its source.
The rain stays the same substance even though its form changes: vapour, cloud, drop.

ex.q: Explain the water cycle as shown in the poem.
st: Evaporation: rain rises unseen from land and sea.
Condensation: it changes form in the sky, yet stays the same.
Precipitation: it falls to wash the droughts and dust of the earth.
Return: it gives back life to its origin.
ex.a: Rain rises as vapour, forms clouds, falls as rain on dry land and returns to its source, again and again.

topics.rl: IMD tracks this very cycle: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal moisture rises, forms monsoon clouds over the Western Ghats, and falls on fields across India.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)
topics.t: Rain the life-giver
topics.h: A seed can lie in the soil for months waiting. One shower, and it cracks open. Whitman's rain knows its power.
p: Without rain, seeds would remain only seeds: latent (hidden, inactive) and unborn.
Rain gives back life to its own origin: the earth and sea from which it rose.
It makes the earth pure and beautiful, by day and by night, forever.
Rain gives selflessly: it asks for nothing and returns again and again.
'Strange to tell': surprisingly, the rain gave an answer. The phrase marks the wonder of a shower speaking.

ex.q: What is meant by 'strange to tell'?
st: Rain is not expected to speak.
Yet it answers the poet.
So the poet calls it strange, a wonder worth telling.
ex.a: It means 'surprisingly', since it is strange that the rain could reply.

topics.rl: Indian farmers watch the first monsoon showers before sowing kharif crops; without rain, the seeds in the soil remain latent, exactly as the poem says.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)
topics.t: Rain and song: the bracketed lines
topics.h: A song leaves a singer's heart, travels to listeners who may or may not care, and still comes back with love. Whitman says rain does the same.
p: The last two lines, in brackets, compare rain to a song.
A song issues from its birthplace (the poet's heart), wanders, is heard or ignored ('reck'd or unreck'd'), and duly returns with love.
Analogy: rain rises from the earth and returns to it; poetry or music rises from the poet and returns to bless the world.
Metaphor: rain as the Poem of Earth; simile-like comparison: rain is like a song.
Why brackets? They mark the poet's own comment, set apart from the rain's voice.

ex.q: What analogy does the poem draw between rain and music?
st: Rain: rises from earth and sea, falls back to give life.
Song: rises from the poet's heart, reaches the world, returns with love.
Both complete a cycle and give without demanding.
ex.a: Both rise from a source, travel, enrich others and return to their origin, whether noticed or not.

topics.rl: A song by Lata Mangeshkar or A.R. Rahman leaves the studio, travels everywhere, and returns as love from listeners. That is the bracketed lines' idea.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)
topics.t: Devices: personification, archaic words, free verse
topics.h: Rain that speaks, words like 'thou' and 'art', and lines that refuse to rhyme: Whitman's poem is full of tools examiners love.
p: Personification: the rain speaks and describes its own journey.
Archaic language: thou (you), art (are), reck'd/unreck'd (heeded/unheeded), lave (wash), drouths (droughts), atomies (tiny particles).
Free verse: no fixed rhyme or metre; inversion of normal word order (e.g., 'said I' for 'I said').
Parentheses (brackets) set apart the poet's closing comment.
Alliteration and imagery: 'said I to the soft-falling shower' repeats the s sound; 'bottomless sea' and 'dust-layers of the globe' give vivid pictures.

ex.q: Find an inversion in the poem and rewrite it in normal order.
st: Inversion: 'said I to the soft-falling shower'.
Normal order puts subject before verb.
Rewrite: 'I said to the soft-falling shower'.
ex.a: 'Said I' becomes 'I said'.

topics.rl: Old Hindi film songs and bhajans often use poetic inversion and old words; poets choose them to sound timeless, as Whitman did.

topics.ch: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)
topics.t: Rain poems and extract practice
topics.h: Rain has inspired poets everywhere, from Kalidasa's 'Meghaduta', with a cloud as messenger, to Tagore's monsoon songs. Comparing poems is a great way to see what makes Whitman's special.
p: Try this out: find other poems on rain and compare their mood, imagery and message with Whitman's.
Kalidasa's 'Meghaduta' uses a cloud as a messenger; Tagore wrote many songs of the monsoon. Whitman's rain is a voice and a poet.
Extract questions often test: the water cycle, personification, the meaning of 'strange to tell', and the bracketed lines.
When comparing poems, look at speaker, imagery, devices and theme.

ex.q: Compare: In one poem rain is a destroyer (floods); in Whitman's it is a life-giver. What is the key difference?
st: Identify the role of rain in each.
Whitman: gives life and beauty, returns to its origin.
Other: brings danger and loss.
ex.a: Whitman celebrates rain as a selfless creator; the other poem shows its destructive side.

topics.rl: In Indian languages there are countless monsoon songs, such as Hindi 'barkha' songs. Comparing them with Whitman shows rain's many faces.

topics.t: When did my childhood go? Rationalism
topics.h: Was there one day you stopped being a child? Markus Natten's poem keeps asking that question, and each answer is a step towards growing up.
p: 'Childhood' by Markus Natten reflects on the moment childhood is lost.
Four stanzas; the refrain 'When did my childhood go?' (a rhetorical question) structures the poem; each of the first three stanzas offers a possible answer.
Stanza 1 asks: was it the day he ceased to be eleven? Or the time he realised that Hell and Heaven could not be found in geography (on a map), and so could not exist?
This is rationalism: he began to think logically and to question beliefs that cannot be proved.
Rhetorical questions are asked for effect, not for an answer; repetition makes the search feel urgent.

ex.q: What does the line about Hell and Heaven not being in geography suggest?
st: Geography deals with real places on a map.
Hell and Heaven are not on any map.
So the child begins to reason that they may not be real: logical thinking.
ex.a: It marks the start of rational thinking: he questions ideas he cannot locate or prove.

topics.rl: A Class 6 student who starts asking 'But how do we know?' about everything is showing the rationalism Natten describes. Science classes at school feed it.

topics.t: Hypocrisy and a mind of his own
topics.h: Adults say 'share with others' and then fight over a parking spot. Spotting that gap is, says the poet, another sign that childhood is ending.
p: Stanza 2: perhaps childhood went when he saw that adults were not all they seemed to be.
They talked of love and preached of love, but did not act so lovingly: he recognised their hypocrisy.
Stanza 3: perhaps it went when he found his mind was really his own, to use whichever way he chose.
His thoughts were no longer borrowed from others but his own and his alone: individuality and independent thinking.
Stanza map: Stanza 1 – rationalism; Stanza 2 – hypocrisy of adults; Stanza 3 – individuality.

ex.q: Identify the stanzas that deal with individuality, rationalism and hypocrisy.
st: Stanza 1: Heaven and Hell not in geography – rationalism.
Stanza 2: adults preach love but don't act lovingly – hypocrisy.
Stanza 3: his mind is his own – individuality.
ex.a: Rationalism – Stanza 1; hypocrisy – Stanza 2; individuality – Stanza 3.

topics.rl: Many Indian teens notice when elders say 'don't use phones at dinner' and then scroll themselves. Noticing that gap, and forming your own views, is part of growing up.

topics.t: Where did childhood go? Stanza 4 and devices
topics.h: Look at a baby's face and you'll see it: total trust, total wonder. The poet says that's where his childhood went.
p: Stanza 4 changes the question from 'when' to 'where': where did my childhood go?
Answer: it went to some forgotten place hidden in an infant's face; that is all he knows.
Metaphor: childhood is a thing that has gone to a 'forgotten place'.
Nostalgia: childhood survives only in the innocence of an infant, which he can see but not regain.
Contrast between a child's and an adult's view; end rhyme in parts (e.g., eleven/Heaven, place/face). The poet's feeling: wistful longing for lost innocence.

ex.q: What is the poet's feeling about childhood?
st: He searches for the moment it was lost.
He accepts it is gone.
He sees it only in an infant's innocent face.
ex.a: He feels nostalgic and wistful; childhood is precious and lost, surviving only in a baby's innocence.

topics.rl: Watch a toddler at a Diwali mela staring at lights with pure wonder. Adults can't get that back, which is exactly what Stanza 4 says.

topics.t: Growing up: themes and exam practice
topics.h: Growing up isn't a birthday; it's a set of discoveries. The poem lists three, and exam questions love asking you to name them.
p: Main theme: loss of innocence and the process of growing up.
Growing up involves three stages: rationalism (logical questioning), recognising hypocrisy, and individuality (independent thought).
Growing up is gradual, not one fixed day; that is why the poet keeps asking 'when?'.
Most poetic lines (personal choice): many readers pick the infant's-face lines, because they turn a vague loss into a vivid, tender image.
Exam tips: extract MCQs on stages and devices; short answers (40–50 words) on what growing up involves.

ex.q: What, according to the poem, does growing up involve?
st: Questioning beliefs logically (rationalism).
Seeing that adults don't always practise what they preach (hypocrisy).
Learning to think for oneself (individuality).
ex.a: Growing up means learning to reason, recognising adult hypocrisy, and developing one's own mind.

topics.rl: Psychologists describe adolescence as a time of questioning and forming identity: the same stages Natten lists in verse.

topics.t: What if Panipat went the other way?
topics.h: In 1761 the Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat. Now imagine a world where they won. A historian wakes up in exactly that world.
p: Jayant Narlikar was an Indian astrophysicist and science-fiction writer, and the founder-director of IUCAA, Pune.
'The Adventure' is science fiction built on alternate history, catastrophe theory and quantum theory.
Professor Gangadharpant Gaitonde, a historian, travels on the Jijamata Express from Pune towards Bombay and finds himself in a world where history has taken a different path.
Clues: the train carriages carry 'GBMR' and a small Union Jack; at the border station Sarhad an Anglo-Indian officer checks permits; Bombay has British-style shops and banks.
In this world the Marathas won the Third Battle of Panipat (1761); in real history they lost it to Ahmad Shah Abdali.

ex.q: What is 'alternate history' in this story?
st: Real history: the Marathas lost at Panipat in 1761.
Story world: the Marathas won.
The story imagines how India would differ after that change.
ex.a: It imagines a different course of history, here a Maratha victory at Panipat, and explores its results.

topics.rl: Narlikar spent decades at TIFR and IUCAA, Pune. His Marathi science fiction made physics fun for Indian readers, just as this story does.

topics.t: History rewritten: the bullet that missed
topics.h: A single bullet, a few inches off target, and the map of India looks completely different. That's the idea behind this world.
p: In the Town Hall library Gaitonde reads history volumes; they match his knowledge until the Battle of Panipat.
In this world a bullet narrowly missed Vishwasrao (the Peshwa's son and heir); in real history he was killed.
Led by Sadashivrao Bhau (Bhausaheb) and Vishwasrao, the Marathas won and drove Abdali back to Kabul; their morale and power soared.
The East India Company shelved its expansion and was confined to pockets near Bombay, Calcutta and Madras; the Peshwas kept a puppet Mughal ruler in Delhi.
Later India developed elected, democratic institutions and stood on its own feet; Bombay stayed a British outpost under a 1908 lease due to end in 2001.

ex.q: How did Vishwasrao's survival change history in the story?
st: Real history: his death at Panipat demoralised the Marathas and they lost.
Story: the bullet missed, the Marathas won.
Result: no British conquest; India built its own institutions.
ex.a: His survival led to a Maratha victory, halted British expansion and let India develop without becoming a British colony.

topics.rl: Cricket fans know this feeling: one dropped catch at a critical moment can change a whole World Cup. History has such moments too.

topics.t: Gaitonde in Bombay: the library and Azad Maidan
topics.h: A historian in a strange city does what historians do: he goes to the library. Then he goes to a public meeting, and that is where things go wrong.
p: At the Forbes building he looks for his son Vinay, but no one by that name works there: in this world his son may not exist.

At the Town Hall library he reads the history volumes and finds the point where history changed: Panipat. He finds the Bakhar account of the bullet missing Vishwasrao and, by mistake, pockets the book.
At Azad Maidan he finds a public lecture with an empty president's chair; in this world such meetings have no presiding person.
He sits in the chair and starts speaking about why a president is needed; the angry audience pelts him with tomatoes and eggs and tries to throw him out.
He vanishes from the crowd and is back in his own world; his collision with a truck had first sent him across, and he had been missing for two days.

ex.q: Why did the audience at Azad Maidan get angry with Gaitonde?
st: Meetings in that world were held without a president.
Gaitonde sat in the empty chair and insisted a president was needed.
The audience saw this as breaking their custom and threw things at him.
ex.a: Because he occupied the president's chair and lectured them, against their custom of meetings with no presiding chair.

topics.rl: Mumbai's Azad Maidan is a real ground near CST where rallies and meetings are held, and the Asiatic Society's library is in the Town Hall. Narlikar uses real landmarks.

topics.t: Rajendra explains: catastrophe and quantum theory
topics.h: Is it possible to be in two worlds? Rajendra Deshpande answers with two real scientific ideas, and a clever guess about a truck.
p: Rajendra Deshpande, a scientist friend, explains Gaitonde's experience using two theories.
Catastrophe theory: a small change at a critical point can cause a sudden, large change in outcome. Vishwasrao's death at Panipat was such a turning point.
Quantum theory: an electron's behaviour cannot be predicted with certainty (lack of determinism); many possible states or worlds may exist, and an observer experiences one at a time.
Many-worlds idea: two realities exist side by side; Gaitonde made a transition from one to the other, like an electron jumping between states.
Trigger: just before his collision with the truck, Gaitonde was thinking about catastrophe theory and the Battle of Panipat; that may have acted as the trigger.

ex.q: Explain catastrophe theory with the story's example.
st: A system near a critical point can change suddenly.
At Panipat, Vishwasrao's death was such a point.
If he survives, the outcome flips: the Marathas win.
ex.a: Small changes at critical moments can cause huge changes; Vishwasrao living or dying decided the whole battle.

topics.rl: A small crack in a dam or a single delayed signal on the Mumbai suburban railway can cascade into a huge outcome. Catastrophe theory studies such tipping points.

topics.t: Themes: one event, two Indias
topics.h: After being pelted with tomatoes in another world, Gaitonde makes a very practical decision: no more chairing meetings. Ever.
p: Gaitonde decides never to preside over a meeting again; he withdraws from presiding at the Panipat seminar.
Reason: in the other world, sitting in the president's chair led to humiliation; the memory is too fresh.
Theme 1: a single event (one bullet) can change a nation's history.
Theme 2: reality versus perception; is reality only what we experience through our senses?
Theme 3: history, science and philosophy each search for truth, using records, experiments and reasoning respectively.

ex.q: Why did Gaitonde decide never to preside over meetings again?
st: He sat in the president's chair at Azad Maidan.
The audience humiliated him and threw him out.
So he resolved to avoid presiding in future.
ex.a: Because presiding at Azad Maidan led to his humiliation; he wanted to avoid any repeat.

topics.rl: Students of history in India often debate 'what if' questions, like what if 1857 had succeeded. Such debates show how one event shapes everything after it.

topics.t: Vocabulary and exam practice
topics.h: 'De facto', 'astute', 'relegated', 'gave vent to': learn these and you can describe any political drama, real or alternate.
p: Blow-by-blow account = detailed step-by-step report; de facto = in reality, though not officially; morale booster = something that raises confidence.

Astute = shrewd and clever; relegated to = pushed to a lower position; doctored accounts = falsified records; political acumen = sharp political judgement; gave vent to = expressed (a feeling) openly.

Textbook true/false: the story is not an account of real events (F); it hinges on a historical event (T); Rajendra is not a historian (F); the places are not all imaginary (F); it relates history to science (T).

Explain statements: the two Indias are two possible worlds; Gaitonde's 'catastrophic experience' was being pulled into another world; his research gave him first-hand evidence of an alternate history.
Long answer: link catastrophe theory with alternate history using Vishwasrao's survival; debate whether one event can change history.

ex.q: Use 'relegated to' correctly about the Company in the story.
st: Relegated to = pushed to a lower position.
In the story, the Company lost power.
Sentence: The East India Company was relegated to a few trading pockets.
ex.a: The East India Company was relegated to a few small pockets near Bombay, Calcutta and Madras.

topics.rl: News channels give a 'blow-by-blow account' of an India–Pakistan match; politicians are praised for 'political acumen'. These phrases are everyday English.

topics.t: Setting out from Ravu
topics.h: Imagine a road trip where the 'highway' is a dirt track at over 5,000 metres, your car shares the plains with wild asses, and your goal is to walk around a sacred mountain.
p: Nick Middleton is a British geographer and travel writer; 'Silk Road' is an extract from his travelogue.
It records his journey across Tibet to perform the kora, the circuit around Mount Kailash; the title recalls the ancient Silk Road trade route.
He leaves Ravu with Tsetan, a skilful driver, and Daniel, who helps and translates and later heads back to Lhasa.
Landscape: open plains, the dark tents of nomads, flocks tended by solitary drokbas, a few gazelles and herds of wild asses.
Tibetan words: kora (pilgrimage circuit), drokba (nomad herder), kyang (Tibetan wild ass).

ex.q: Who are Tsetan and Daniel, and what do they do?
st: Tsetan: the hired driver who handles the tough roads.
Daniel: a travel companion who helps and translates.
Daniel later leaves to go back to Lhasa.
ex.a: Tsetan is the expert driver; Daniel is the helpful companion who leaves at Hor for Lhasa.

topics.rl: Indian pilgrims on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, organised by the Ministry of External Affairs via Lipulekh or Nathu La, cross the same high Tibetan plateau.

topics.t: Mastiffs, a short cut and the thin air
topics.h: At 5,515 metres, there's about half the oxygen of sea level. Your head throbs, your car slides on snow, and huge black dogs chase your wheels.
p: Tibetan mastiffs, big fearless dogs, guard nomad tents; they were prized at China's imperial courts as hunting dogs and sent as tribute along the Silk Road.
Tsetan takes a short cut heading south-west, almost directly towards Kailash, across high passes.
Snow blocks the track: Tsetan crosses one patch and drives around another, cutting off a hairpin bend; the top of the pass, at 5,515 m, is marked by a cairn of rocks.
The author suffers a throbbing headache from altitude sickness; he gulps water from his bottle on the climb, and the headache clears as they descend.

Phrases: ducking back (pulling back quickly), swathe (broad strip), careered down (moved fast, out of control), manoeuvres (skilful movements), cairn (pile of stones as a marker), salt flats (flat salty land), billowed (swelled out).

ex.q: Why were Tibetan mastiffs popular in China's imperial courts?
st: They were big, strong and fearless.
They made excellent hunting dogs.
So they were sent as tribute along the Silk Road.
ex.a: Because they were valued as powerful hunting dogs and were sent to the courts as tribute.

topics.rl: Indian Army soldiers at Siachen and Ladakh are acclimatised for days because of altitude sickness. Drinking water and climbing slowly help, just as the author found.

topics.t: Hor and the sacred lake
topics.h: Some places look magical in old books and disappointing in real life. Hor, on the shore of a holy lake, was one of those for the author.
p: At Hor, Daniel leaves them to hitch a ride back to Lhasa.
Hor is a grim, miserable place: no vegetation, just dust, rocks and rubbish.
The Japanese monk Ekai Kawaguchi, who reached Lake Mansarovar in 1900, was so moved by its sanctity that he burst into tears.
Contrast: the legendary, sacred beauty of Mansarovar versus the dismal reality of Hor on its shore.
Mansarovar is Tibet's most venerated lake; in Hindu and Buddhist belief it is linked with the sources of great rivers (the Sutlej actually flows from it).

ex.q: Why does the author find Hor such a contrast to what Kawaguchi described?
st: Kawaguchi found the lake spiritually overwhelming and wept.
The author finds Hor grim, dusty and littered.
The spiritual image clashes with the dirty modern town.
ex.a: Kawaguchi saw holy beauty, but the author sees a dirty, dismal town; legend and reality clash.

topics.rl: Indian pilgrims still take a holy dip in Mansarovar on the Kailash Yatra. Like the author, many are struck by the gap between the sacred lake and the rough towns around it.

topics.t: Darchen: a cold, a doctor and Norbu
topics.h: Stuck in a cold, dirty town with a blocked nose, unable to sleep, and no pilgrims in sight: then a stranger walks in who wants to do the same trek.
p: Darchen, at the foot of Kailash, is dirty and cold; the author has a heavy cold, a blocked nose and trouble breathing, and stays awake all night.
At Darchen's medical college a Tibetan doctor diagnoses a cold and altitude effects; Tsetan translates, and the doctor gives him a course of Tibetan medicine.
Speaking 'through' someone means communicating via an interpreter, as the author speaks to the doctor through Tsetan.
There are no pilgrims yet because the season has not begun; the author is disappointed.
He meets Norbu, a Tibetan scholar working in Beijing, who also plans the kora; when Norbu suggests going together, the author feels his 'positive thinking' has worked.
