ex.q: What does 'I spoke to the doctor through Tsetan' mean?
st: The author does not speak Tibetan.
Tsetan translates both ways.
So Tsetan is the interpreter.
ex.a: The author communicated with the doctor with Tsetan acting as interpreter.

topics.rl: Foreign tourists in rural India often speak 'through' a local guide who translates. The idea is the same as at Darchen.

topics.t: The kora and the meaning of the journey
topics.h: Why would anyone walk around a mountain at over 5,000 metres? For millions of believers across four faiths, the answer is simple: Kailash is sacred.
p: Kora: the circumambulation of Mount Kailash, sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of Bon.
Travel is both a physical challenge (altitude, cold, rough roads) and a spiritual quest.
Myth versus reality: legends of sacred, exotic places meet dusty towns and discomfort.
Hill people's kindness: Lhamo's farewell gift, Tsetan's care and skill, the doctor's help; and human endurance in harsh land.
Adjective-noun pairs: shaggy monsters, brackish (slightly salty) lakes, rickety (shaky) table, hairpin (very sharp) bend, rudimentary (basic) general stores.

ex.q: Why is the journey both physical and spiritual?
st: Physical: altitude sickness, snow, cold, rough tracks.
Spiritual: the goal is the kora of a sacred mountain.
The hardship itself becomes part of the pilgrimage.
ex.a: The author endures physical hardship to reach a sacred goal, so the trip tests body and spirit.

topics.rl: The Kedarnath and Amarnath yatras show the same mix: hard climbs, cold and thin air, done out of deep faith.

topics.t: Reasons, comments and exam practice
topics.h: 'Give reasons' and 'comment on' questions are where students lose marks by being vague. This lesson shows the exact points examiners want.
p: Title: refers to the old Silk Road trade routes across the region, along which goods and even Tibetan mastiffs (as tribute) travelled.

Reasons: mastiffs prized as hunting dogs; Hor disappointing against its sacred image; Darchen disappointing because of illness and no pilgrims; positive thinking 'working' when Norbu proposed teaming up.

Comments: purpose of the journey (the kora); his health at Darchen; meeting Norbu; Tsetan's steady support; Tsetan's joke that, as a Buddhist, the author's death would not matter much, but would be bad for business.
Discussion: hill folk are often kind and sensitive; people take hard journeys for faith, adventure or self-discovery; legends often differ from reality.
Long answer: travel as a test of endurance, using altitude, snow, illness and determination.

ex.q: Comment on Tsetan's role in the journey.
st: Skilful driver on snowy, risky tracks.
Translator and helper at the doctor's.
Brings humour and calm; his Buddhist joke lightens the mood.
ex.a: Tsetan is the author's skilled driver, interpreter and caring support, adding calm and humour.

topics.rl: Sherpa guides on Everest expeditions play Tsetan's role: driver, guide, translator and morale-booster rolled into one.

topics.t: Strangers in the same house
topics.h: Living under one roof for years and still talking like strangers: many families know that silence. Elizabeth Jennings puts it into a father's voice.
p: Elizabeth Jennings was an English poet; in 'Father to Son' the speaker is a father talking about his grown son.
Form: four stanzas of six lines each; each stanza follows the same rhyme pattern (abbaba), though many rhymes are only half-rhymes (child/build/killed).
The father says he does not understand his son, even though they have lived together in the same house for years.
He admits he knows nothing of him and tries to build a relationship from memories of how the son was when small.
They speak like strangers; there is no sign of understanding between them.

ex.q: Who is the speaker, and what is his problem?
st: The speaker is a father.
He has lived with his son for years.
Yet he cannot understand him; they talk like strangers.
ex.a: A father who, despite years in the same house, cannot understand or connect with his grown son.

topics.rl: In many Indian homes, parents and teens spend hours under one roof yet talk little beyond 'Have you eaten?'. The poem captures that gap.

topics.t: Seed, land and what the son loves
topics.h: A father who planted a seed, only to find the land it grew on now belongs to someone else. Jennings packs a generation gap into one farming metaphor.
p: The father wonders if he has wasted the 'seed' he spent, or sown it in land that is the son's and not his.
Metaphors: 'seed' = his child, the effort and love he invested; 'land' = the son's own world, which the father cannot enter.
The son is 'built to my design' (like the father), yet what the son loves, the father cannot share.
Silence surrounds them; neither can reach the other.
Lines showing their difference: 'what he loves I cannot share'; 'we speak like strangers'; the son making and moving his own world.

ex.q: Explain the metaphor of the seed and the land.
st: Seed: the son, and the love and effort the father put into him.
Land: the son's own life and world.
The father fears his seed grew in land that is no longer his.
ex.a: The father invested himself in his son, but the son has grown into his own world, outside the father's reach.

topics.rl: Indian parents often say 'we sowed, now you reap'. In the poem the harvest grows in a field the father can no longer enter.

topics.t: The prodigal son and anger from grief
topics.h: In a famous Bible parable, a son who wasted everything comes home and is welcomed with a feast. The father in this poem almost wishes for that story.
p: The father would rather have his son prodigal, returning to his father's house, the home he knew, than see him make and move his own world.
Biblical allusion: the parable of the prodigal son, who leaves, wastes his inheritance and returns home to be forgiven by his father.
The father says he would forgive him too, shaping a new love out of sorrow.
Father and son must live on the same globe and the same land: they cannot escape each other.
Paradox: the father cannot understand why anger grows from grief; sorrow at the distance turns into anger.

ex.q: What is the allusion to the prodigal son, and why is it used?
st: Parable: a son leaves, wastes his inheritance, returns, and is forgiven.
The father wishes his son would 'return' like that.
It shows his longing to forgive and reconnect.
ex.a: It refers to the Bible's prodigal son; the father wishes his son would come back so he could forgive him and love him anew.

topics.rl: In many Indian families, a child who moves to another city and stops calling is welcomed back with open arms on Diwali. That is the 'prodigal' longing.

topics.t: An empty hand: helplessness and hope
topics.h: Two people, each holding out an empty hand, each waiting for the other to make the first move. The poem ends right there.
p: Ending: father and son each put out an empty hand, longing for something to forgive.
'Empty hand' (metaphor): an offer of peace with nothing yet to give, and a sign of helplessness.
The father's helplessness: he cannot understand, cannot share, cannot even explain his own anger; he can only wish and wait.
He also shows possessiveness (wanting the son back in his house) and a longing for reconciliation.
Rhyme and repetition: each stanza follows the same abbaba pattern, but with many half-rhymes; the repeated word 'understand' stresses the gap; imagery of silence fills the poem.

ex.q: How is the father's helplessness shown?
st: He says he does not understand his son.
He cannot share what the son loves.
He cannot understand his own anger; he can only hold out an empty hand.
ex.a: Through his repeated failure to understand, his inability to share and his empty, waiting hand.

topics.rl: Family counsellors in Indian cities often say the first step is just reaching out, even when you have no perfect words. The empty hand is that first step.

topics.t: Generation gap: personal or universal?
topics.h: The poem never names the father or son, their country or their quarrel. That silence makes it everyone's story.
p: Theme: the generation gap and the lack of communication between parent and child.
Family misunderstanding is universal: it happens across cultures and times.
Personal or universal? Spoken as one father's experience, but with no names or specific details, so it reads as universal.
Exam focus: extract questions on metaphors (seed, land, empty hand), allusion, paradox and tone; short answers on the generation gap.

ex.q: Is the poem about a personal or a universal experience?
st: It is spoken by one father in the first person.
It has no names, places or specific quarrels.
Many families feel the same gap.
ex.a: Though personal in voice, it describes a universal experience of parents and children growing apart.

topics.rl: From joint families in Kolkata to nuclear families in Bengaluru, parents and teens everywhere argue about careers, phones and friends: a universal gap.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse
topics.t: Four a.m., a white horse and an honest tribe
topics.h: Your cousin taps on your window at four in the morning, sitting on a beautiful white horse. Your family is famous for honesty, and you're pretty sure he didn't buy it.
p: William Saroyan was an Armenian-American writer; the story is set among Armenian immigrants in Fresno, California.
It is told in the first person by Aram, aged nine, in a warm, comic tone.
Mourad, Aram's thirteen-year-old cousin, wakes him at four in the morning, sitting on a beautiful white horse.
Their Garoghlanian tribe was poor but famous for honesty; for them, stealing was unthinkable.
So Aram is torn: he longs to ride the horse, but he knows Mourad could not have bought it.

ex.q: What is the central conflict for Aram when he sees the horse?
st: He has always longed to ride a horse.
His family is poor, so Mourad could not have bought it.
His tribe is famous for honesty; stealing is unthinkable.
ex.a: His desire to ride clashes with his family's strict honesty.

topics.rl: Many Indian families take great pride in their 'naam', their good name for honesty. Aram's tribe guards its name in exactly that way.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse
topics.t: Borrowing, not stealing? Mourad's way with horses
topics.h: Aram's logic: it isn't stealing if you plan to give it back. Is that honesty, or a nine-year-old's clever excuse?
p: Aram reasons it is not stealing, because they do not mean to sell the horse; they will return it. Stealing a horse for a ride is not the same as stealing for money, he decides.
Mourad has a way with animals: the horse obeys him, and he rides with ease.
When Aram tries to ride alone, the horse runs wild and throws him off.
They hide the horse in the barn of a deserted vineyard that once belonged to the farmer Fetvajian.
Aram: innocent, eager, admiring of Mourad. Mourad: adventurous, with the family's 'crazy streak', and a natural animal lover.

ex.q: How does Aram convince himself that riding the horse is not stealing?
st: Stealing means taking something to keep or sell.
They only want to ride it.
They plan to return it, so in his mind it is not stealing.
ex.a: He decides it is not stealing because they will not sell the horse and mean to give it back.

topics.rl: Borrowing a friend's cycle without asking 'just for a ride' happens in many Indian colonies. Saroyan asks whether intention changes what the act is.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse
topics.t: John Byro visits and Uncle Khosrove roars
topics.h: A farmer sadly reports his missing horse; the boys' uncle loses his temper and shouts the same line he always shouts. Comedy, Armenian style.
p: John Byro, an Assyrian farmer, visits Aram's family and says his white horse was stolen a month ago.
He complains that without the horse his surrey is useless and he has had to walk.
Uncle Khosrove interrupts with his favourite line: 'It is no harm; pay no attention to it.' He even asks what the loss of a horse is, when they have all lost their homeland.
Uncle Khosrove: a huge, loud, impatient man with an enormous moustache, who shouts the same line at every problem.
Comic effect: his outbursts are exaggerated and repeated, making him a figure of fun while hinting at the pain of exile.

ex.q: Write a short character sketch of Uncle Khosrove.
st: Appearance: huge, with a famous moustache.
Manner: loud, impatient, angry.
Habit: repeats 'It is no harm; pay no attention to it.'
Effect: comic, yet shows exile's pain.
ex.a: Uncle Khosrove is a loud, impatient giant whose repeated cry 'It is no harm; pay no attention to it' makes him comic.

topics.rl: Every Indian family has an uncle with one favourite line, said at every crisis. Uncle Khosrove is that uncle.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse
topics.t: The meeting on the road and the horse's return
topics.h: A farmer looks into a horse's mouth, recognises it, and then decides to trust the boys' family instead of his own eyes. That's the story's quiet turning point.
p: On the road the boys meet John Byro; he examines the horse's teeth and says it looks exactly like his horse.
But he says he knows their parents and their family's honesty; the horse must be the twin of his, and he will trust his heart rather than his eyes.
Next morning the boys return the horse to Byro's vineyard.
Later Byro tells the family that his horse came back, better-tempered and stronger than before.

Why didn't Byro accuse them? He trusted the family's honour, did not want to shame them, and gave them a chance to return it. Remorse or fear? Their prompt return suggests conscience and family pride.

ex.q: Why didn't John Byro accuse the boys, though he recognised the horse?
st: He respected the Garoghlanians' honesty.
He did not want to shame the boys or their family.
He gave them a chance to return it themselves.
ex.a: Out of respect for their family's honesty, and to let the boys put things right without disgrace.

topics.rl: Many Indian shopkeepers let a regular customer's child take something on credit, trusting the family name. Byro's trust works the same way.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse
topics.t: Themes: honesty, temptation and borrowing
topics.h: Taking a horse for a joyride: harmless fun or theft? This story makes you laugh and then quietly makes you decide.
p: Honesty and family pride: the tribe's reputation is the story's moral test; temptation pushes against it.
Childhood longing and innocence: Aram's dream of riding a horse is pure and strong.
Stealing versus borrowing: the boys tell themselves it is borrowing, but they hide it and keep it for weeks without permission.
Humour and warmth: comic characters (Mourad, Khosrove), gentle irony and affection for immigrant family life.
Moral judgment: keeping the horse secretly for weeks was not fully honest; returning it was the honest act that redeemed them.

ex.q: Was it honest of the boys to keep the horse for weeks?
st: They did not ask the owner.
They hid the horse, which shows they knew it was wrong.
But they meant to return it, and they did.
ex.a: Not fully: keeping it secretly was wrong, but their return of the horse showed their honesty in the end.

topics.rl: The Indian Penal Code and its successor, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, both treat dishonestly taking movable property without consent as theft. Even 'just borrowing' without consent can count.

topics.t: An address remembered: Marconistraat 46
topics.h: During a war, a family hands its treasured things to an acquaintance for 'safe keeping'. Years later, the daughter goes to collect them.
p: Marga Minco was a Dutch writer of Jewish origin who survived the Second World War; most of her family did not.
'The Address' is a first-person story about loss and memory after the war; it uses flashbacks to the war years.
After the war the narrator goes to an address her mother once gave her: Mrs Dorling, Marconistraat number 46.
Mrs Dorling, an old acquaintance of the mother, had taken away the family's valuables during the war, saying she would keep them safe.
The mother had told the daughter the address in case she ever needed it.

ex.q: Why does the narrator go to Marconistraat 46?
st: During the war, Mrs Dorling took the family's possessions.
She said she would keep them safe.
After the war, the narrator goes to see them.
ex.a: To see the family possessions Mrs Dorling had taken during the war for 'safe keeping'.

topics.rl: During Partition in 1947 many families left homes and goods with neighbours, hoping to return. Stories of going back to such addresses echo Minco's tale.

topics.t: The first visit: a closed door and a green cardigan
topics.h: The door opens a crack. The woman wears your mother's green cardigan. And she won't let you in.
p: On the first visit Mrs Dorling opens the door only a little and asks, 'Have you come back?'
She is wearing the narrator's mother's green knitted cardigan with wooden buttons; she refuses to let the narrator in.
Flashback: the mother had explained that Mrs Dorling came and carried away cutlery, plates and other things, saying she would save them.
'Have you come back?' reveals that Mrs Dorling did not expect anyone to return; she is uneasy, unwelcoming and does not want to give anything back.
Mrs Dorling's character: greedy, opportunistic and cold.

ex.q: What does Mrs Dorling's greeting 'Have you come back?' reveal?
st: She recognises the narrator.
She is surprised, as if she expected the family never to return.
She shows no warmth or concern; she wants to keep the things.
ex.a: It shows she did not expect the family to survive or return, and that she is unwelcoming and wants to keep their belongings.

topics.rl: Holocaust museums from Amsterdam to Washington tell of neighbours who 'kept' Jewish families' goods and never returned them. Minco's story is about that betrayal.

topics.t: The second visit: familiar things, strange room
topics.h: You finally enter the room and see your mother's things on a stranger's table. Instead of joy, you feel only that you want to leave.
p: On a second visit Mrs Dorling's daughter, a girl of about fifteen, lets the narrator in while her mother is out.
The narrator sees familiar things: the tablecloth with a burn mark, the pewter plate, the silver cutlery, the Hanukkah candle-holder.
She is shocked to see them used as ordinary household things.
In strange surroundings the objects have lost their value; they are cut off from the life and memories they belonged to.
The visit leaves her feeling that the room, not the objects, now owns them; she wants only to get away.

ex.q: Why did the objects lose their value for the narrator?
st: They were in a stranger's house, not her family home.
They had no link to her mother or her old life there.
Without that context, they felt ordinary and empty.
ex.a: Out of their family setting, the objects no longer carried the memories that made them precious.

topics.rl: A grandparent's brass lota or old radio is precious in your home; in a shop window it's just another object. The meaning lives in the setting and the memories.

topics.t: Forgetting the address: letting go
topics.h: She came to reclaim her past. She leaves deciding to forget the address altogether. Is that defeat, or freedom?
p: The narrator leaves without taking anything and decides to forget the address.
Why: the objects were linked to a life that no longer exists; seeing them in strange surroundings hurt; she chose to move on.
Narrator: dignified, thoughtful and mature; she does not quarrel and learns to let go.
The mother: trusting and practical; she handed things to Mrs Dorling believing they would be safe. Her death in the war is implied, not stated.
The mother's fate: she did not survive the war, which is why only the daughter returns.

ex.q: Why does the narrator decide to forget the address?
st: The objects no longer carried their old meaning.
They reminded her painfully of a lost life.
She chose to move on rather than live in the past.
ex.a: Because the objects had lost their meaning and only brought pain; she chose to let go and move on.

topics.rl: Many refugees, such as families uprooted by Partition, speak of deciding not to go back to their old houses. Letting go can be a way to survive.

topics.t: Themes: war, memory and betrayal
topics.h: War takes lives, then takes the small things that held lives together: a tablecloth, a candle-holder, a cardigan. Minco's story is about that second loss.
p: War and Holocaust trauma: loss of family, home and belongings during the Second World War.
Memories attached to objects: things carry memories, but only in their right setting.
Moving on from the past: the narrator chooses to let go.
Greed and betrayal: Mrs Dorling profits from others' suffering; the value of objects lies in their context.
Exam focus: short answers on the visits and objects; long answer on war, memory and letting go.

ex.q: Long answer plan: 'Objects have value only in their context.' Discuss with reference to 'The Address'.
st: Intro: the narrator seeks her family's belongings after the war.
Body 1: in Mrs Dorling's house the objects feel strange.
Body 2: they are cut off from the people and life they belonged to.
Body 3: she leaves them and forgets the address.
Conclusion: memory, not objects, holds value.
ex.a: Objects carry meaning through the people and places they belong to; without that context, they lose value.

topics.rl: Gandhi's spectacles and charkha are precious because of their story, not their material. Context gives objects meaning.

topics.t: The Pearsons at home
topics.h: She cooks, irons, waits on everyone and is thanked by no one. Then her neighbour suggests a magic trick that will change everything.
p: J.B. Priestley was an English novelist and dramatist; 'Mother's Day' is a one-act comic play.
Setting: the living room of the Pearson family's house, on an afternoon in early autumn.
Mrs Annie Pearson is taken for granted by her husband George, her daughter Doris and her son Cyril.
She is meek and self-sacrificing: she runs after them, irons their clothes and waits up for them, but never complains to their faces.
The play will show her learning to be firm.

ex.q: What is Mrs Pearson's problem at the start of the play?
st: She works hard for her family.
Her husband and children take her for granted.
She is too meek to stand up for herself.
ex.a: Her family treats her as a servant, and she is too gentle to assert herself.

topics.rl: National surveys in India show women spend several hours a day on unpaid household work. Priestley's play, written decades ago, still feels current.

topics.t: Mrs Fitzgerald and the Eastern spell
topics.h: Enter the neighbour: a bold Irish fortune-teller who smokes, speaks her mind, and knows a spell from her years in the East.
p: Mrs Fitzgerald, the neighbour, is a bold, confident Irish fortune-teller who urges Mrs Pearson to assert herself and be the boss.
Mrs Pearson is too timid to do it; so Mrs Fitzgerald suggests they swap personalities using a spell she learnt in the East.
They hold hands, she murmurs the spell, and their personalities exchange bodies: a fantasy body swap.
Mrs Fitzgerald is the catalyst: the person who triggers change.
Devices: fantasy (body swap), dramatic irony (the audience knows of the swap, the family does not) and slapstick humour.

ex.q: What is dramatic irony in this play?
st: The audience knows the two women have swapped.
The family does not know.
So we laugh as they react to 'Mother's' strange behaviour.
ex.a: The audience knows Mrs Fitzgerald is inside Mrs Pearson's body while the family doesn't: that gap creates dramatic irony.

topics.rl: Indian films like 'Chaalbaaz' or TV comedies use swapped identities for laughs. Priestley's play uses the same fantasy trick.

topics.t: Mrs Fitzgerald in charge: the family is shocked
topics.h: Imagine coming home and your gentle mother is smoking, drinking stout, playing cards and refusing to make tea. Welcome to the Pearson household.
p: Mrs Fitzgerald, now in Mrs Pearson's body, smokes, drinks stout and refuses to serve the family.
She mocks Doris's date with Charlie Spence and refuses to iron her clothes; she rebukes Cyril for his careless demands.
She shocks George by telling him people at the club laugh at him behind his back and call him 'Pompy-ompy Pearson'.
The family is stunned; they begin to apologise and offer help.
George: self-important; Doris: selfish; Cyril: careless and demanding.

ex.q: How does 'Mrs Pearson' (Mrs Fitzgerald inside) treat George?
st: She refuses to obey him.
She tells him the club members laugh at him.
She reveals his nickname 'Pompy-ompy Pearson'.
ex.a: She shocks his pride by revealing that people laugh at him and mock him with a nickname.

topics.rl: Many Indian homes saw the same shift when a mother went on 'strike' for a day: suddenly everyone noticed how much she did.

topics.t: Swapping back: the real Mrs Pearson takes charge
topics.h: The magic wears off and the real Mrs Pearson is back. The question is: has she learnt anything?
p: The two women swap back; the real Mrs Pearson returns to her own body.
Mrs Fitzgerald warns her not to go soft; Mrs Pearson now firmly sets the terms.
Ending: the family agrees to stay at home, play a game of rummy and help with supper, while Mrs Pearson and George have a talk.
Role reversal brings change: the family sees what it is like to be treated as they treated her.
Is the solution realistic? The magic is fantasy, but the lesson (being firm earns respect) is realistic. One-act structure, stage directions and comic dialogue keep it brisk.

ex.q: How does the role reversal bring change?
st: The family is treated the way they treated her.
They feel shock and shame.
When she returns, she uses this to set firm terms.
ex.a: By being treated harshly, the family realises its selfishness, and Mrs Pearson learns to be firm.

topics.rl: Workplace role-swap days in Indian companies, where managers do junior jobs for a day, rely on the same idea: experience teaches empathy.

topics.t: Themes: respect for homemakers
topics.h: No salary, no holidays, no thank-you. Priestley's comedy makes a serious point about the work that keeps families running.
p: Homemakers' work is often taken for granted; the play asks for respect and recognition.
Role reversal and self-assertion: standing up for yourself can change how others treat you.
Humour and satire on family life: Priestley mocks selfish habits through comedy.
Relevance today: in many families, unpaid home work, mostly done by women, is still undervalued; sharing chores and showing appreciation matter.

ex.q: Is the play relevant to today's families?
st: Home chores are still often done by one person.
That work often goes unthanked.
The play's message about respect and sharing still applies.
ex.a: Yes: unequal, unappreciated housework still exists, so the play's message remains relevant.

topics.rl: Campaigns in India encourage families to share housework, and many schools run 'help at home' projects. Priestley's message fits right in.

topics.t: How the humour works, and exam practice
topics.h: Why is it funny when a mother drinks stout and scolds her husband? Because we never expect it. Comedy runs on surprise, contrast and exaggeration.
p: Humour comes from role reversal (meek mother turned bossy), contrast with expectation, exaggeration, dramatic irony and sharp comic dialogue.
The nickname 'Pompy-ompy Pearson' and the family's shocked faces add verbal and situational comedy.
Character sketches: Mrs Pearson (meek, then firm); Mrs Fitzgerald (bold catalyst); George (pompous); Doris (selfish); Cyril (careless).
Long answer: the dignity of homemakers and the need for respect; use incidents from before and after the swap.

ex.q: Write a short character sketch of Mrs Fitzgerald.
st: Who: Mrs Pearson's Irish neighbour, a fortune-teller.
Traits: bold, confident, plain-speaking.
Role: catalyst; uses a spell to teach the family a lesson.
ex.a: Mrs Fitzgerald is a bold, outspoken fortune-teller whose spell and firm behaviour make the Pearsons respect their mother.

topics.rl: Indian sitcoms like 'Sarabhai vs Sarabhai' use the same comic tools: exaggerated characters, sharp lines and role clashes.

topics.t: A young doctor's long night begins
topics.h: It's nearly midnight. A young doctor walks home, and a worried man is pacing outside his door. His wife's first baby is coming, after twenty years of waiting.
p: A.J. Cronin was a Scottish doctor and novelist; 'Birth' is an extract from his novel 'The Citadel'.
The hero is Dr Andrew Manson, a young doctor newly qualified, working in a Welsh mining town.
Returning home near midnight after an evening out, Andrew finds Joe Morgan waiting for him.
Joe's wife Susan is expecting their first baby after nearly twenty years of marriage.
This becomes Andrew's first truly critical case.

ex.q: Why is this case so important to the Morgans?
st: They have been married for nearly twenty years.
This is their first child.
So the baby means everything to them.
ex.a: After almost twenty years of waiting, it is their first baby, so the stakes are huge.

topics.rl: Doctors at rural PHCs across India often face their hardest cases at night, with few resources, just like Andrew in a mining town.

topics.t: A stillborn child and a collapsing mother
topics.h: After hours of labour, the baby is born without a breath, and the mother herself is in danger. Andrew has seconds to decide whom to save first.
p: Andrew stays through a long, difficult labour; Susan's mother waits nearby.
The baby is born stillborn, showing no sign of life, and Susan collapses.
Andrew first works on the mother, reviving her, because she is in serious danger.
Only after she is stable does he turn to the baby, refusing to give up on it.
Joe Morgan: anxious, restless husband. Susan's mother: hopeful, patient and quietly brave.

ex.q: Why did Andrew attend to the mother before the baby?
st: Susan had collapsed and could die.
The baby already seemed lifeless.
A doctor saves the life most clearly at risk first, then tries for the other.
ex.a: Because Susan's life was in immediate danger; once she was stable, he turned to save the baby.

topics.rl: In Indian emergency rooms, doctors use triage: treat the patient in most immediate danger first. Andrew's decision follows the same logic.

topics.t: Hot water, cold water: bringing a baby to life
topics.h: A memory from his student days, two basins of water and half an hour of desperate work: that's all Andrew has to save a life.
p: Andrew sees that the baby has asphyxia pallida (white asphyxia): limp, pale and not breathing.
He recalls a case he had seen at the Samaritan hospital in his training and the method used there.
He plunges the baby alternately into a basin of hot water and a basin of cold water, and rubs and presses its chest rhythmically.
After about half an hour of effort, the baby gasps and begins to breathe.
Andrew feels that at last he has truly been of use, that he has done something real.

ex.q: Describe the method Andrew used to revive the baby.
st: Diagnosis: asphyxia pallida, a limp, pale, breathless baby.
Alternate dips in hot and cold water to shock the body.
Rub and press the chest rhythmically to start breathing.
Keep going for about half an hour until the baby breathes.
ex.a: He alternated the baby between hot and cold water, rubbing and pressing its chest, until it breathed after about half an hour.

topics.rl: Today newborn resuscitation in Indian hospitals follows protocols like NRP, using bag-and-mask ventilation. Cronin's story shows how much early doctors relied on memory and grit.

topics.t: Duty, persistence and the meaning of 'Birth'
topics.h: Andrew went into that night as a young doctor unsure of himself. He came out knowing why he'd chosen medicine.
p: Andrew Manson: dedicated, determined and humane; he refuses to give up when others would.
Themes: duty and perseverance; medical ethics (saving life, not giving up); the miracle of life and the triumph of persistence.
His emotional state moves from tense worry during the labour, to desperate determination over the baby, to joy and fulfilment.
The case changes him: he feels for the first time that he has done something real and useful.
Title 'Birth': the birth of the baby, and also the 'birth' of Andrew as a true doctor.

ex.q: Explain the significance of the title 'Birth'.
st: Literal: a baby is born and brought to life.
Figurative: Andrew is 'born' as a real doctor.
Both lives begin anew that night.
ex.a: It refers to the baby's birth and to Andrew's rebirth as a confident, committed doctor.

topics.rl: Many young doctors at AIIMS and district hospitals describe one case that made them feel truly like doctors. Andrew's night is that case.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Tale of Melon City
topics.t: A just and placid king builds an arch
topics.h: A king orders an arch to impress his people. On its first day, it knocks his crown off. What happens next is one of the funniest chains of blame in English verse.
p: Vikram Seth is an Indian poet and novelist (author of 'A Suitable Boy' and 'The Golden Gate'); 'The Tale of Melon City' is a humorous narrative ballad.
Form: rhyming couplets (pairs of rhyming lines) with simple, comic storytelling.
A king described as 'just and placid' orders an arch to be built across the main road, to edify (improve and instruct) the spectators.
The workmen build it, but the arch is too low: when the king rides under it, it knocks off his crown.
The king calls this a disgrace and orders that the chief of builders be hanged.

ex.q: Why did the arch become a problem?
st: The king ordered an arch across the main road.
It was built too low.
As he rode under it, it knocked off his crown.
ex.a: It was built so low that it struck the king's crown off as he passed under it.

topics.rl: Indian cities have grand gateways like India Gate and the Gateway of India. Imagine one built too low for the VIP car: that's the comic start of this poem.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Tale of Melon City
topics.t: Pass the blame!
topics.h: Builders blame workmen, workmen blame bricks, masons blame the architect, and the architect blames... the king. It's the world's oldest office game.
p: The chief of builders blames the workmen.
The workmen blame the bricks, saying they were of the wrong size; the masons blame the architect.
The architect reminds the king that he himself had made amendments to the plans.
Confused, the king summons the wisest man in the land, so old he cannot walk or see; he declares that the arch itself is to blame and must be hanged.
Ballad style: each round of blame-passing repeats the same pattern, building comedy through repetition.

ex.q: Trace the chain of blame.
st: Chief of builders → workmen.
Workmen → bricks (wrong size).
Masons → architect.
Architect → the king's own amendments.
Wise man → the arch.
ex.a: Builders blame workmen, workmen blame bricks, masons blame the architect, the architect blames the king, and the wise man blames the arch.

topics.rl: When a new flyover leaks, every agency blames another: contractor, engineer, designer. The poem's chain of blame feels very familiar.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Tale of Melon City
topics.t: A noose, a hanged king and a melon on the throne
topics.h: The crowd wants a hanging. The noose is set high. Guess who's the only one tall enough? And then an idiot picks the next king.
p: The arch cannot be hanged: a councillor points out it had touched the king's head, so hanging it would be shameful.
The restless crowd demands that someone be hanged; the king agrees that someone must hang, and guilt can be settled later.
The noose is set high, people are measured, and only the king is tall enough to fit it; so the king is hanged by royal decree.
By custom, the next person to pass the City Gate chooses the new ruler; an idiot passes and answers 'A melon', his answer to every question.
A melon is crowned king; the people don't mind, as long as they are left in peace and liberty.

ex.q: How did the king end up being hanged?
st: The crowd demanded a hanging.
The noose was set high, and people were measured for it.
Only the king was tall enough, so he was hanged by royal decree.
ex.a: The noose was too high for everyone except the king, so he himself was hanged.

topics.rl: Indian folk tales of Akbar–Birbal and Tenali Raman also mock foolish rulers and odd justice. Seth's ballad belongs to the same comic tradition.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Tale of Melon City
topics.t: Satire, irony and humour
topics.h: A 'just' king who hangs innocent men, a 'wise' man who blames an arch, a melon on the throne: every line of this poem winks at the reader.
p: Satire on foolish rulers and absurd justice: the king punishes without thinking and ends up hanged himself.
Passive citizens: the people accept anything, even a melon king, as long as their peace and liberty continue.
Irony and humour about power and governance: the 'just and placid' king acts rashly; the 'wisest man' blames an object.
Devices: satire, irony, humour and rhyming couplets carry the comic tale.
Instances of humour and irony: the arch knocking off the crown; the chain of blame; the king fitting the noose; the melon king.

ex.q: Find two instances of irony in the poem.
st: The 'just' king orders hangings without proper inquiry.
The king who demanded a hanging is himself hanged.
The 'wisest' man blames a lifeless arch.
ex.a: The 'just' king acts unjustly and ends up hanged by his own rule; the wisest man blames an arch.

topics.rl: Political cartoons in Indian newspapers, from R.K. Laxman's Common Man onwards, use the same satire: rulers who act foolishly and citizens who quietly put up with it.

topics.ch: Snapshots: The Tale of Melon City
topics.t: Tell the tale, judge the state
topics.h: Exam favourites: narrate the tale in your own words, judge a 'just and placid' king, and say how peace and liberty can be kept. Here's how to ace them.
p: Narrate in your own words: arch ordered → too low → crown knocked off → chain of blame → wise man blames arch → arch spared → crowd wants a hanging → king fits noose → idiot chooses melon → people content.
Impression of a state with a 'just and placid' king: on the surface calm and fair, but the king's rash decisions show a foolish, unpredictable rule.
Peace and liberty are maintained by fair laws, careful inquiry before punishment, accountable leaders and alert, responsible citizens.
Short answers: the chain of blame and the choice of the melon king.

ex.q: Board question: How can peace and liberty be maintained in a state?
st: Rulers must be just and think before acting.
Laws must be fair, with proper inquiry before punishment.
Citizens must be alert and responsible, not passive.
ex.a: Through wise, accountable rulers, fair laws and inquiry, and citizens who stay alert and responsible.

topics.rl: India's Constitution protects liberty through rights, courts and elections; the poem shows, by contrast, what happens when justice is a whim.

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Portrait of a Lady'?
qa.e: The memoir is by Khushwant Singh, about his own grandmother.

qa.q: In which person is 'The Portrait of a Lady' narrated?
qa.e: The grandson tells the story as 'I', recalling his own experiences.

qa.q: Which description of the grandmother is correct?
qa.e: The author describes her as short, fat and slightly bent with a wrinkled face.

qa.q: What colour did the grandmother always wear?
qa.e: She always dressed in spotless white, which matches her serene, pure image.

qa.q: Where does the story begin?
qa.e: The narrator first lived with his grandmother in the village while his parents lived in the city.

qa.q: The text is best classified as a:
qa.e: It is a true, first-person portrait of a real person, which is a memoir or character sketch.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The title 'The Portrait of a Lady' is gently ironic. Reason (R): The 'lady' is a simple, old, deeply religious grandmother, not a fashionable woman.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: A 'portrait of a lady' suggests elegance; the subject is a simple old woman, so the title is ironic, and R gives exactly that reason.

qa.q: Which of these was Khushwant Singh NOT known as?
qa.e: He was a writer, journalist and historian; he was not a professional singer.

qa.q: What was striking about the grandfather's portrait?
qa.a: He looked at least a hundred years old
qa.e: The portrait showed a big turban, loose clothes and a long white beard, making him look about a hundred.

qa.q: The grandmother is compared to a winter landscape in the mountains. This is an example of:
qa.e: The comparison uses 'like', so it is a simile.

qa.q: What quality does the 'winter landscape' comparison bring out?
qa.e: The white, still mountain scene suggests peace, purity and contentment.

qa.q: Why does the author say she was beautiful though not pretty?
qa.a: Her beauty came from her inner peace and faith
qa.e: Her looks were plain, but her calm, faith and goodness made her beautiful.

qa.q: The idea of the grandmother as a young, pretty girl seemed to the author:
qa.e: He jokes that it was hard to believe and almost revolting to imagine; this is gentle humour.

qa.q: The phrase 'not pretty but beautiful' shows a contrast between:
qa.e: Pretty refers to outward appearance; beautiful refers to her inner qualities.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The narrator could not imagine his grandmother as young. Reason (R): The grandmother always dressed in spotless white.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but her white clothes are not why he could not picture her young; that was because she had always looked old to him.

qa.q: What did the grandfather wear in the portrait?
qa.a: A big turban and loose clothes
qa.e: He wore a big turban and loose-fitting clothes and had a long white beard.

qa.q: Why did the grandmother sing her prayers while dressing the boy?
qa.a: She hoped he would learn them by heart
qa.e: She sang in a monotonous sing-song, hoping he would pick up the prayers.

qa.q: Where was the village school?
qa.e: The village school was attached to the temple, and the priest taught there.

qa.q: What did the grandmother do while the boy was in class?
qa.a: Read the scriptures inside the temple
qa.e: She sat inside the temple reading the scriptures and walked him home afterwards.

qa.q: What did they feed the village dogs?
qa.e: They carried stale chapattis for the dogs on the way home.

qa.q: Feeding the dogs every day shows that the grandmother was:
qa.e: Daily feeding of dogs shows compassion for animals.

qa.q: What did the boy carry to school?
qa.a: A wooden slate, an ink-pot and a reed pen
qa.e: He used a wooden slate, an earthen ink-pot and a reed pen, typical of a village school then.

qa.q: Why did the boy live with his grandmother in the village?
qa.a: His parents were living in the city
qa.e: His parents had settled in the city, and the boy stayed with his grandmother until they sent for them.

qa.q: In this phase of their relationship, the grandmother and the boy were:
qa.e: In the village they spent the whole day together; this was the closest phase of their friendship.

qa.q: How did the narrator travel to his city school?
qa.e: He went by motor bus, so she could not accompany him.

qa.q: Which subject did the grandmother NOT want him to miss?
qa.e: She was upset that the school taught nothing about God and the scriptures.

qa.q: Which of these did the narrator learn at the English school?
qa.e: He told her about the law of gravity, Archimedes' principle and the earth being round.

qa.q: Why could she no longer help him with his lessons?
qa.a: They were in English and Western science
qa.e: She did not know English or Western science, so she could not help.

qa.q: What was the effect of the move to the city on their friendship?
qa.e: The city move began the drift; they shared a room but were no longer constant companions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The grandmother was unhappy with the English school. Reason (R): It taught Western science and English but nothing about God or the scriptures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Her unhappiness came from the absence of religious teaching, as R states.

qa.q: Which detail shows the generation gap most clearly?
qa.a: She disliked his lessons on gravity
qa.e: Her dislike of modern science lessons shows the clash of old and new values.

qa.q: Who sent for the narrator and his grandmother to come to the city?
qa.e: His parents had settled in the city and sent for them.

qa.q: Why did the music lessons disturb the grandmother?
qa.a: She thought music was not for gentlefolk
qa.e: She believed music was for harlots and beggars, not respectable people.

qa.q: What happened after she learnt about the music lessons?
qa.a: She rarely spoke to him after that
qa.e: She fell silent; it was the last straw in that phase of their friendship.

qa.q: What became her favourite pastime in the city?
qa.e: In the city house she fed the sparrows that came in hundreds.

qa.q: How did the sparrows behave with the grandmother?
qa.e: They trusted her completely and perched all over her; she smiled and did not shoo them away.

qa.q: Which word best describes her silence after the music lesson?
qa.e: Her silence was a quiet way of showing she disapproved.

qa.q: Why is the music lesson an important moment in their friendship in the city?
qa.a: after it she rarely spoke to him
qa.e: The real turning-point was the move to the city; the music lesson deepened the break, and after it she rarely spoke to him.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the city the grandmother found comfort in the sparrows. Reason (R): She had lost her grandson's company and needed something to love.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: With the boy drifting away, she turned her affection towards the sparrows.

qa.q: What did she feed the sparrows?
qa.e: She broke bread into little bits for the sparrows.

qa.q: What snapped when the narrator went to university?
qa.e: With a room of his own, the common link of their friendship snapped.

qa.q: 'She accepted her seclusion with resignation' means she:
qa.e: Resignation here means calm acceptance of something one cannot change.

qa.q: How long did he stay abroad?
qa.e: He went abroad for further studies for five years.

qa.q: How did she behave at the station when he left?
qa.e: She showed no emotion; her lips moved in prayer and her fingers counted beads.

qa.q: Why did he treasure her kiss on his forehead?
qa.a: He felt it might be their last physical contact
qa.e: Given her age, he feared he might not see her again.

qa.q: Which was NOT part of her daily life after he grew up?
qa.e: Walking him to school belonged to the village phase, not to this later phase.

qa.q: Her calm at the station most likely shows:
qa.e: Her calm was rooted in faith and self-control, not in lack of love.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The grandmother complained bitterly about her loneliness. Reason (R): She spent her days spinning, praying and feeding sparrows.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: She never complained (A is false), and R correctly describes her days.

qa.q: How did she receive him on his return?
qa.a: She clasped him in her arms, praying
qa.e: She came to the station, hugged him, and her lips moved in prayer.

qa.q: What did she do on the evening of his return?
qa.a: She beat an old drum and sang
qa.e: She collected the neighbourhood women, beat an old drum and sang for hours.

qa.q: What were her songs about?
qa.e: She sang of warriors coming home, fitting her grandson's return.

qa.q: Why did the family persuade her to stop singing?
qa.a: To stop her from overstraining herself
qa.e: She was old, and hours of drumming could exhaust her.

qa.q: What was unusual that evening for the first time?
qa.a: She did not say her prayers
qa.e: She missed her prayers for the first time the narrator had known her.

qa.q: What did the doctor say about her fever?
qa.a: It was mild and would go
qa.e: The doctor called it a mild fever that would pass; she thought differently.

qa.q: Why did she refuse to talk on her last morning?
qa.a: She wanted her last hours for prayer
qa.e: Having missed her prayers, she did not want to waste more time talking.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Missing her prayers hints that her end is near. Reason (R): She missed her prayers because the doctor told her to rest.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Missing prayers does foreshadow her death, but she missed them while celebrating with the drum, not on a doctor's orders.

qa.q: How did she die?
qa.a: Peacefully, praying and telling her beads
qa.e: Her lips stopped moving in prayer and the rosary fell from her fingers.

qa.q: What was the colour of the shroud?
qa.e: The family covered her with a red shroud, as is customary.

qa.q: How many sparrows came?
qa.e: Thousands of sparrows sat around the body in the room and verandah.

qa.q: Who threw bread crumbs to the sparrows?
qa.e: His mother threw crumbs, which the birds ignored.

qa.q: What did the sparrows do when the body was carried away?
qa.e: Once the body was taken, the sparrows flew away quietly.

qa.q: The silent sparrows are best seen as a symbol of:
qa.e: The birds she fed now mourn her, showing the bond between humans and nature.

qa.q: What happened to the crumbs the next morning?
qa.a: The sweeper swept them into the dustbin
qa.e: The crumbs lay untouched until the sweeper swept them away.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The sparrows ignored the bread crumbs. Reason (R): They were not hungry that evening.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: They ignored the crumbs out of grief, as the story suggests, not because they were full.

qa.q: Which incident best shows she was deeply religious?
qa.a: She prayed and told her beads constantly
qa.e: Constant prayer and bead-telling directly show her devotion.

qa.q: Which trait is proved by her feeding sparrows and dogs?
qa.e: Feeding animals daily shows compassion and kindness.

qa.q: Her objection to music lessons shows that she was:
qa.e: Her views came from traditional ideas of what was respectable.

qa.q: How did she face death?
qa.e: She knew her end had come and spent her last hours peacefully in prayer.

qa.q: Which word best describes how she accepted loneliness?
qa.e: She accepted her seclusion with quiet resignation.

qa.q: Which pair is a correct trait-proof match?
qa.a: Caring – she bathed and dressed the boy
qa.e: Bathing and dressing him each morning shows care.

qa.q: Was the grandmother a strong character? The best answer is:
qa.a: Yes; she bore loneliness and death with dignity
qa.e: Her calm acceptance of separation and death shows inner strength.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The grandmother was self-reliant. Reason (R): She filled her lonely days with her own routine and never complained.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Her self-made routine and lack of complaint prove her self-reliance.

qa.q: Which theme is shown by the clash over music and science lessons?
qa.e: The lessons represent modern education, which clashes with her traditional values.

qa.q: What happens to the relationship as the narrator grows up?
qa.e: They drift apart in daily life, yet affection survives.

qa.q: Which event best shows the bond between humans and nature?
qa.e: The birds she fed sit silently around her body.

qa.q: How does the grandmother cope with ageing and loneliness?
qa.e: Spinning, praying and feeding sparrows help her cope calmly.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The story shows a generation gap. Reason (R): The grandmother learnt English so she could help with his lessons.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: The generation gap is real, but she never learnt English; she could not help with his English lessons.

qa.q: Which line of thought is a fair reading of the story?
qa.a: The old adapt to change quietly
qa.e: The story shows her adapting quietly; it does not preach any extreme view.

qa.q: The grandmother can be seen as a symbol of:
qa.e: Her habits and beliefs represent an older generation.

qa.q: Which detail best proves that her love for him never faded?
qa.a: Her joyful drumming on his return
qa.e: Her joyful celebration shows deep love even after years apart.

qa.q: 'She told her beads' means she:
qa.e: To tell beads is to count them while praying.

qa.q: In 'I can't tell the difference', 'tell' means:
qa.e: Here 'tell' means to recognise or distinguish.

qa.q: 'A few moments of respite' means:
qa.e: Respite means a brief relief from work or trouble.

qa.q: 'The sagging skins of the dilapidated drum' suggest the drum was:
qa.e: Dilapidated means in a state of disrepair, old and worn.

qa.q: The humour in imagining the grandparents as children comes from:
qa.a: the contrast with their very old looks
qa.e: Having seen them only as very old, the idea of them as playful children seems absurd.

qa.q: How is the story organised?
qa.e: It moves forward in time through clear phases.

qa.q: 'The thought was almost revolting' here means the idea seemed:
qa.e: Revolting here means disgusting or unacceptable, used humorously.

qa.q: Which word best replaces 'seclusion' in 'she accepted her seclusion'?
qa.e: Seclusion means being alone, cut off from others: isolation.

qa.q: 'She took to feeding sparrows' means she:
qa.a: began it as a regular habit
qa.e: 'Take to' means to start doing something as a habit.

qa.q: 'She was taken ill' means she:
qa.e: 'Take ill' means to become sick.

qa.q: Which verb best suits an old woman walking with difficulty?
qa.e: Hobble means to walk with difficulty or a limp.

qa.q: A proud, showy walk is called a:
qa.e: Swagger is a confident, arrogant way of walking.

qa.q: Choose the correct sentence.
qa.a: She had prayed every day until that evening.
qa.e: An action continuing up to a past point takes the past perfect 'had prayed'.

qa.q: Why is the past perfect useful in a memoir?
qa.a: It marks the earlier of two past events
qa.e: Memoirs move between layers of the past; the past perfect marks the earlier layer.

qa.q: Which language did the narrator most likely speak with his grandmother?
qa.e: They lived in a Punjab village, so Punjabi was their home language.

qa.q: Which is the best opening for a descriptive portrait of a loved person?
qa.a: Dadu's laugh filled our kitchen each morning.
qa.e: A vivid, specific detail draws the reader in; the others are generic or vague.

qa.q: A student translates 'tooti-phooti dholak' from Hindi into English for the homecoming scene. Which phrase from the story fits best?
qa.e: 'Tooti-phooti' means old and falling apart, which is exactly what 'dilapidated' means; she beat such a drum while singing of warriors' homecoming.

qa.q: Extract: she walked with a hand on her waist 'to balance her stoop'. What does 'stoop' show?
qa.a: Her bent posture due to age
qa.e: A stoop is a forward bend of the back, showing old age.

qa.q: Extract: her other hand was busy 'telling the beads'. This shows she was:
qa.e: Telling the beads of a rosary is part of prayer.

qa.q: Which is the best 40–50 word answer opening for 'Why was the grandmother upset at the city school?'
qa.a: The school taught nothing about God or scriptures.
qa.e: It answers the question directly in the first line.

qa.q: For a long answer on 'the grandmother as a symbol of the old generation', which point is most relevant?
qa.e: Her views on education show the values of her generation.

qa.q: The best evidence for the theme of the changing relationship is:
qa.a: the three phases of their bond
qa.e: The three phases chart how their relationship changed.

qa.q: In an extract MCQ about tone, the description of the grandparents as young seems:
qa.e: The narrator jokes lightly about the idea.

qa.q: What should a strong conclusion of a long answer do?
qa.a: Tie the points back to the main theme
qa.e: A conclusion links the body points to the theme.

qa.q: Which statement about the title would earn marks?
qa.a: It is ironic: a simple old woman is a 'lady'
qa.e: A 'lady' suggests elegance; she is simple and saintly, hence the irony.

qa.q: Who wrote 'A Photograph'?
qa.e: The poem is by the British poet Shirley Toulson.

qa.q: How old was the mother in the photograph?
qa.e: She was the big girl, some twelve or so.

qa.q: Who were Betty and Dolly?
qa.e: Betty and Dolly were the girl cousins holding her hands.

qa.q: Who took the photograph?
qa.e: All three smiled at the uncle with the camera.

qa.q: What were the girls doing in the photograph?
qa.e: They went paddling, walking in shallow water.

qa.q: How many stanzas does the poem have?
qa.e: There are three stanzas, each a different time phase.

qa.q: Which best describes the form of 'A Photograph'?
qa.e: It has no regular rhyme or metre: free verse.

qa.q: The poem is mainly a reflection on:
qa.a: a photo of the poet's late mother
qa.e: It reflects on the poet's mother through an old photograph.

qa.q: What does 'cardboard' literally refer to?
qa.a: The stiff mount of an old photo
qa.e: Old photographs were pasted on card mounts.

qa.q: What is suggested by calling the photo 'cardboard'?
qa.a: The moment is frozen and lifeless
qa.e: A flat card holds only a still image of a living moment.

qa.q: What did the camera capture?
qa.a: A happy moment of three girls
qa.e: It caught the three girls paddling and smiling.

qa.q: 'Transient' means:
qa.e: Transient means lasting only a short time.

qa.q: A 'wry' smile is one that is:
qa.a: dryly amused and a little sad
qa.e: Wry suggests a twisted, bittersweet amusement.

qa.q: 'Laboured' in the poem suggests something:
qa.e: Laboured means forced or effortful, not natural.

qa.q: In the poem, 'circumstance' refers to:
qa.e: 'This circumstance' is the fact of the mother's death.

qa.q: 'Paddling' in the poem means:
qa.e: The girls waded in the shallow sea.

qa.q: What has changed less over the years, according to the poem?
qa.e: The sea appears to have changed less than the people.

qa.q: Why are the girls' feet called 'transient'?
qa.e: Transient stresses how briefly human beings live compared with the sea.

qa.q: How many years after the holiday did the mother laugh at the photo?
qa.e: The poem places her laughter twenty or thirty years later.

qa.q: What amused the mother about the photograph?
qa.a: The way they were dressed for the beach
qa.e: She laughed at the old-fashioned beach clothes.

qa.q: The sea holiday was the mother's past. What is the poet's past?
qa.e: The poet remembers her mother laughing at the photo.

qa.q: What does the mother's laugh at the snapshot indicate?
qa.a: Fond nostalgia with a hint of loss
qa.e: She enjoys the memory but knows that time is gone.

qa.q: The contrast in Stanza 2 is between:
qa.e: The unchanged sea is set against the ageing girls.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The poem shows the sea changing faster than the people. Reason (R): Nature outlasts the short lives of human beings.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: The sea 'appears to have changed less', so A is false; R states the poem's real idea.

qa.q: Who are 'both' in 'Both wry with the laboured ease of loss'?
qa.e: Both the mother (remembering childhood) and the poet (remembering her mother) feel loss.

qa.q: What does 'laboured ease' suggest?
qa.a: Calm that takes effort to show
qa.e: The ease is forced; underneath lies sadness.

qa.q: What has the mother lost, as she looks at the photo?
qa.e: She looks back on a childhood that is gone.

qa.q: What has the poet lost?
qa.e: The poet has lost her mother, and with her, her mother's laughter.

qa.q: How long has the mother been dead?
qa.e: The poem says nearly as many years as that girl lived, which is about twelve.

qa.q: 'There is nothing to say at all' shows that the poet:
qa.e: Her grief is too deep to express.

qa.q: 'Its silence silences' contains a play on the word 'silence'. The effect is to:
qa.e: The repetition shows death's silence spreading to the poet.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The poet has much to say about her mother's death. Reason (R): The silence of death leaves her speechless.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: She says there is nothing to say (A false); R is true.

qa.q: Which is NOT a theme of 'A Photograph'?
qa.e: The poem is personal; it has nothing to do with politics.

qa.q: What triggers the memories in the poem?
qa.e: The poem begins with the cardboard photograph.

qa.q: What does Stanza 1 present?
qa.a: The mother as a girl at the sea
qa.e: Stanza 1 describes the photograph of the mother at about twelve.

qa.q: What does Stanza 2 present?
qa.a: The grown mother laughing at the photo
qa.e: Twenty or thirty years later the mother laughs at the snapshot.

qa.q: What does Stanza 3 present?
qa.a: The poet's grief at her death
qa.e: It speaks of the years since the mother died and the silence of death.

qa.q: The poem contrasts the sea with human beings to show that:
qa.e: The sea's sameness is set against human transience.

qa.q: Through how many time phases does the poem move?
qa.e: The girl at the sea, the grown mother laughing, and the poet after her death.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The poem moves through three time phases. Reason (R): Each stanza focuses on a different stage in time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The three stanzas create the three phases.

qa.q: 'Laboured ease' is an example of:
qa.e: Two contradictory words are placed together.

qa.q: Which device is seen in 'terribly transient'?
qa.e: The 't' sound is repeated at the start of both words.

qa.q: In 'Its silence silences', silence is shown as if it can act. This is:
qa.e: Silence is given the power to silence someone, like a person.

qa.q: The main contrast in the poem is between:
qa.a: changing people and the unchanging sea
qa.e: The poem sets the transient girls against the lasting sea.

qa.q: Extract: the sea 'appears to have changed less' as it washes the girls' 'transient feet'. The tone is:
qa.e: The speaker thinks quietly about time passing.

qa.q: Which visual image comes from Stanza 1?
qa.e: The three girls smiled through their windblown hair at the uncle.

qa.q: What role does the photograph play in the poem?
qa.a: It links the mother's past and the poet's present
qa.e: It connects the girl, the woman and the grieving poet.

qa.q: What are the poet's main feelings in the poem?
qa.e: She remembers her mother fondly and grieves her loss.

qa.q: Who wrote 'We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together'?
qa.e: The account is by Gordon Cook and Alan East.

qa.q: From where did the family set sail?
qa.e: They set sail from Plymouth in July 1976.

qa.q: When did the voyage begin?
qa.e: They set out in July 1976; the storm came in January 1977.

qa.q: Whose voyage were they trying to repeat?
qa.e: They wanted to retrace Captain Cook's voyage of 200 years earlier.

qa.q: How old were Jonathan and Suzanne?
qa.e: Jonathan was six and Suzanne seven.

qa.q: Which description of Wavewalker is correct?
qa.e: Wavewalker was a 23-metre, 30-ton wooden-hulled boat.

qa.q: How many sections does the account have?
qa.e: It moves through three stages: the voyage, the struggle, the rescue.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The family took the voyage seriously. Reason (R): They spent months fitting out Wavewalker and testing her in rough weather.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Their long preparation shows how seriously they planned.

qa.q: Where did Larry and Herb join the voyage?
qa.e: They joined at Cape Town for the rough southern Indian Ocean.

qa.q: What was Herb Seigler's nationality?
qa.e: Herb was Swiss; Larry was American.

qa.q: Why were the crewmen taken on?
qa.a: To help on a very rough ocean
qa.e: The southern Indian Ocean is one of the roughest seas in the world.

qa.q: Where was Christmas celebrated?
qa.a: About 3,500 km east of Cape Town
qa.e: Christmas was held about 3,500 km east of Cape Town.

qa.q: Why did the captain drop the storm jib?
qa.e: Lowering the jib reduced speed in the dangerous sea.

qa.q: What was lashed in a loop across the stern?
qa.e: The mooring rope at the stern helped steady and slow the ship.

qa.q: Which was NOT one of the precautions before the wave struck?
qa.e: Mayday calls came later, in the emergency; the others were precautions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The captain prepared carefully before the storm peaked. Reason (R): He had the crew run the life-raft drill and wear life-lines.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The drill and life-lines are examples of his careful preparation.

qa.q: What happened to the narrator when the wave struck?
qa.e: The wave swept him into the sea before the ship righted.

qa.q: What saved the narrator from drowning?
qa.a: His life-line and the guard rail
qa.e: The life-line pulled tight and he grabbed the guard rails.

qa.q: Which injuries did the narrator suffer?
qa.e: His ribs cracked, and his mouth filled with blood and broken teeth.

qa.q: Who held the wheel after the wave?
qa.e: Mary took the wheel and stayed there through the crucial hours.

qa.q: Through what did water pour into the ship?
qa.a: A broken hatch and a gaping hole
qa.e: The hatch was smashed and the side had a gaping hole.

qa.q: What did the narrator use to cover the holes?
qa.e: He stretched canvas and fitted hatch covers across the gaps.

qa.q: Who pumped water out for hours?
qa.e: The two crewmen pumped tirelessly.

qa.q: A ship that is 'listing' is:
qa.e: Listing means tilting to one side, usually from water inside.

qa.q: What went wrong with the hand pumps?
qa.e: Debris in the water blocked the hand pumps.

qa.q: What happened to the electric pump?
qa.e: The electric pump short-circuited in the flooded ship.

qa.q: How did they finally get a pump working?
qa.a: A spare electric pump was connected
qa.e: The narrator found another electric pump and connected it to an outlet pipe.

qa.q: Which injuries did Sue have?
qa.a: A head bump, black eyes, a cut arm
qa.e: Sue had a huge bump on her head, two black eyes and a deep cut on her arm.

qa.q: Why did Sue not tell her parents about her injury?
qa.a: She did not want to worry her father
qa.e: She told her father she did not want to worry him while he was trying to save them all.

qa.q: Who said they were not afraid to die if they could all be together?
qa.e: Jonathan, the six-year-old son, said this.

qa.q: Why was finding Ile Amsterdam so difficult?
qa.a: It was a tiny island in a vast ocean
qa.e: A small island is a pinprick on a huge ocean, easy to miss.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The narrator's navigation was crucial to their survival. Reason (R): Ile Amsterdam was a large island that was easy to find.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: His navigation was crucial precisely because the island was tiny and easy to miss, so R is false.

qa.q: How did the voyagers feel on 4 January?
qa.e: Pumping had cleared most of the water and they finally ate.

qa.q: How did the situation change on 5 January?
qa.e: The wind returned, and conditions grew desperate.

qa.q: What did Sue's card show?
qa.e: The card had funny drawings of Mary and the narrator, with words of love and thanks.

qa.q: What did Jonathan call his father?
qa.a: The best daddy and best captain
qa.e: He hugged him and called him the best daddy and best captain in the world.

qa.q: Who first spotted Ile Amsterdam?
qa.e: Jonathan and Sue told their father they could see the island.

qa.q: Who welcomed them on Ile Amsterdam?
qa.a: Staff of a French scientific base
qa.e: The island had a French scientific base whose staff helped them.

qa.q: What does 'Land ho!' express?
qa.e: 'Land ho!' is the traditional cry on sighting land.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The children helped keep the family's spirits up. Reason (R): Sue's card and Jonathan's words showed love and faith in their father.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The children's gestures lifted everyone's morale.

qa.q: Which trait best describes the narrator?
qa.e: He keeps thinking, fixes the ship and navigates with little equipment.

qa.q: What was Mary's main role during the storm?
qa.e: Mary steered through the crucial hours.

qa.q: Which phrase best describes Larry and Herb?
qa.e: They pumped for hours without stopping.

qa.q: How did the children react to the danger?
qa.e: Sue hid her injury; Jonathan spoke of facing death together.

qa.q: How do adults and children differ in the text's crisis?
qa.a: Adults show fear; children show trust
qa.e: The adults know the danger; the children trust and comfort them.

qa.q: What is the mood of the third section?
qa.e: It ends with the island sighted and safety reached.

qa.q: Which subtitle best fits Section 2?
qa.e: Section 2 is about pumps, repairs and survival.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The narration shifts in tone across the three sections. Reason (R): Larry Vigil was an American crewman.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but Larry's nationality has nothing to do with the shift in tone.

qa.q: Which is the central theme of the account?
qa.e: The family survives by staying brave and hopeful.

qa.q: Which detail best shows teamwork?
qa.a: Each person had a job to do
qa.e: Larry and Herb pumped, Mary steered, the captain repaired and navigated.

qa.q: The enormous wave represents:
qa.e: The wave shows how small humans are before nature's power.

qa.q: Why do people undertake risky voyages?
qa.a: For adventure and to test limits
qa.e: Thrill, challenge and discovery drive such adventures.

qa.q: What is the main lesson from facing death in the account?
qa.a: Hope and unity help us survive
qa.e: The family's unity and hope saw them through.

qa.q: What did the children's optimism do for the adults?
qa.e: Their words and card gave the adults strength.

qa.q: Which quality of leadership does the narrator mainly show?
qa.e: He calculates, repairs and plans calmly.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Humans can endure great hardship. Reason (R): The family survived days of storm through persistence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Their survival is an example of human endurance.

qa.q: 'Mayday calls' are:
qa.e: Mayday is the international distress call by radio.

qa.q: 'Honing our seafaring skills' means:
qa.e: To hone is to sharpen or improve.

qa.q: 'Ominous silence' suggests:
qa.e: Ominous means threatening, warning of something bad.

qa.q: Which side of a ship is starboard?
qa.e: Starboard is right; port is left.

qa.q: The stern of a ship is its:
qa.e: The stern is the back; the bow is the front.

qa.q: In 'a boom in the IT sector', 'boom' means:
qa.e: In business, a boom is a period of fast growth.

qa.q: A lightship is:
qa.a: a moored ship used as a lighthouse
qa.e: A lightship is moored where a lighthouse cannot be built.

qa.q: 'Pinpricks in the vast ocean' refers to:
qa.e: Small islands look like tiny dots on a huge ocean.

qa.q: 'Catamaran' comes from which language?
qa.e: It comes from Tamil 'kattumaram', meaning tied wood.

qa.q: What does 'kattumaram' literally mean?
qa.e: The boat was made of logs tied together.

qa.q: Which is a boatmen's song tradition from Bengal?
qa.e: Bhatiyali songs were sung by boatmen on Bengal's rivers.

qa.q: Which word is a Hindi word for a storm?
qa.e: Toofan means storm; naav means boat, lehar means wave, kinara means shore.

qa.q: Which question suits a long answer best?
qa.a: How did optimism help them survive?
qa.e: It needs discussion with several points; the others are one-line facts.

qa.q: Extract: Sue said she did not want to worry her father. This shows she was:
qa.e: She put her parents' peace of mind above her own pain.

qa.q: In a short answer on the pumps, which detail is essential?
qa.a: The spare electric pump that worked
qa.e: The key fact is the spare pump that finally worked.

qa.q: Which is the best title-based answer: 'Why is the account called We're Not Afraid to Die...'?
qa.e: The title quotes the son's words, showing the theme of unity and courage.

qa.q: Who wrote 'Discovering Tut: the Saga Continues'?
qa.e: A.R. Williams wrote the feature; the others are people in it.

qa.q: The text is best described as a:
qa.e: It reports real events, research and expert views.

qa.q: About how long ago did Tut die?
qa.e: Tut died some 3,300 years ago.

qa.q: At about what age did Tut die?
qa.e: He was a teenage king who died around nineteen.

qa.q: Tut is described as the last heir of:
qa.e: He was the last of a dynasty that had ruled Egypt for centuries.

qa.q: Which fields does the text combine?
qa.e: It uses science to study an archaeological and historical mystery.

qa.q: Why has Tut's death attracted so much curiosity?
qa.a: He died young and the cause is unclear
qa.e: A young king's unexplained death invites theories.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Scientists scanned Tut's mummy. Reason (R): They hoped to learn more about how he lived and died.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The scan aimed to settle questions about his death and age.

qa.q: For about how long did Amenhotep III rule?
qa.e: He was a powerful pharaoh who ruled for almost forty years.

qa.q: Which god did Akhenaten promote?
qa.e: Akhenaten promoted the worship of the Aten.

qa.q: Where did Akhenaten move the religious capital?
qa.e: He moved it from Thebes to the new city of Akhetaten, now called Amarna.

qa.q: Who called Akhenaten 'wacky'?
qa.e: Egyptologist Ray Johnson described him that way.

qa.q: Which of Akhenaten's acts might be called 'wacky'?
qa.e: He attacked Amun, closed temples and moved the capital, a sharp break with tradition.

qa.q: What was Tut's name at birth?
qa.e: He was born Tutankhaten and became Tutankhamun.

qa.q: What does 'Tutankhamun' mean?
qa.e: His new name honoured Amun.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Tut changed his name from Tutankhaten to Tutankhamun. Reason (R): Amenhotep III ruled for almost forty years.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: Both are true, but the name change was to honour Amun, not because of Amenhotep III's long reign.

qa.q: When did Howard Carter discover Tut's tomb?
qa.e: He found the tomb in 1922.

qa.q: Where was the tomb found?
qa.a: In the Valley of the Kings
qa.e: Tut's tomb was in the Valley of the Kings.

qa.q: What was Howard Carter's nationality?
qa.e: Carter was a British archaeologist.

qa.q: Why were everyday objects like a razor and food buried with Tut?
qa.a: For his use in the afterlife
qa.e: Egyptians believed the dead needed such things in the afterlife.

qa.q: What had cemented the mummy to the coffin?
qa.e: Resins poured during burial had hardened like cement.

qa.q: What did Carter try first to loosen the resins?
qa.a: Placing it in the hot sun
qa.e: He put it in the blazing sun for hours, but that failed.

qa.q: How did Carter's men finally free the mummy?
qa.a: They chiselled the resin and cut it apart
qa.e: They chiselled away resin, removed the head and severed joints.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Carter's team cut the mummy apart. Reason (R): The sun's heat had easily melted the hardened resins.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: They did cut the mummy apart, because the sun had failed to loosen the resins.

qa.q: Why is Carter's work resented today?
qa.a: His methods were crude and damaging
qa.e: His men cut the body apart, showing little respect.

qa.q: How did Carter justify cutting the mummy?
qa.a: Robbers would otherwise take the gold
qa.e: He argued thieves would strip the body of its gold.

qa.q: In which year was the mummy X-rayed?
qa.e: An anatomy professor X-rayed it in 1968.

qa.q: Who X-rayed the mummy in 1968?
qa.e: The text says an anatomy professor did it.

qa.q: What did the 1968 X-ray reveal?
qa.a: His breastbone and front ribs were missing
qa.e: It showed the breastbone and front ribs were missing.

qa.q: Why has Tut's body been examined repeatedly?
qa.e: From X-rays to CT scans, each method could reveal more.

qa.q: How many years after Carter's discovery was the X-ray taken?
qa.e: 1968 is 46 years after 1922: more than forty years.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Carter showed respect for Tut as a person. Reason (R): Carter's men severed the head and joints to free the body.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Cutting the body shows a lack of respect, so A is false; R is a fact.

qa.q: When was Tut's mummy CT-scanned?
qa.e: The scan took place on 5 January 2005.

qa.q: Who led the 2005 scanning?
qa.e: Zahi Hawass of Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities oversaw it.

qa.q: Where was the CT scanner placed?
qa.a: In a trailer near the tomb
qa.e: A portable scanner sat in a trailer close to the tomb.

qa.q: What made the scanner stop briefly?
qa.e: Sand blocked the cooling fan; a substitute fan was used.

qa.q: How many X-ray images did the CT scan take?
qa.e: About 1,700 images were made.

qa.q: What does 'CT' stand for?
qa.e: CT is computed tomography, cross-section X-ray imaging.

qa.q: What happened to the mummy after the scan?
qa.a: It was returned to its tomb
qa.e: Tut was carried back to his tomb after scanning.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 2005 CT scan was carried out in a Cairo hospital. Reason (R): A CT scan builds a 3-D image without cutting the body.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: The scanner stood in a trailer near the tomb, so A is false; R correctly describes CT.

qa.q: What role does science play in the Tut story?
qa.a: It gives evidence about his death
qa.e: Scans give evidence to test theories about Tut.

qa.q: Why were treasures buried with royalty?
qa.e: Egyptians believed the dead needed these objects in the next life.

qa.q: The 'pharaoh's curse' is an example of:
qa.e: It is a belief without evidence.

qa.q: Which is a balanced view on studying mummies?
qa.a: Study them with respect and care
qa.e: Research is valuable but must respect the dead.

qa.q: Which tension does the text explore?
qa.e: It weighs knowledge against respect for the dead.

qa.q: Why might technology give more conclusive evidence than guesswork?
qa.e: Imaging gives precise data that can be checked.

qa.q: What did ancient Egyptians believe about death?
qa.e: Their burial customs show belief in an afterlife.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Superstitions like the curse are not supported by science. Reason (R): Science relies on evidence that can be tested.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Untested beliefs fail the evidence test that science uses.

qa.q: 'Dark-bellied clouds scudded across the sky.' 'Scudded' means:
qa.e: To scud is to move quickly, driven by wind.

qa.q: 'Funerary treasures' are objects:
qa.e: Funerary relates to burial or funerals.

qa.q: 'Circumvented' means:
qa.e: To circumvent is to avoid or get around a problem.

qa.q: An ECG records:
qa.e: ECG stands for electrocardiogram.

qa.q: Which test examines a body after death?
qa.e: An autopsy, or post-mortem, examines a dead body.

qa.q: Why do languages become extinct?
qa.e: When people stop speaking a language, especially to children, it dies out.

qa.q: Which is the best way to preserve an endangered language?
qa.a: Teach it to children and record it
qa.e: Use and documentation keep a language alive.

qa.q: Which topic suits a long answer from this lesson?
qa.e: It needs discussion; the others are short facts.

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Laburnum Top'?
qa.e: Ted Hughes, the British Poet Laureate, wrote it.

qa.q: Ted Hughes is best known for poems about:
qa.e: His poems often focus on animals and the natural world.

qa.q: In which month is the poem set?
qa.e: The poem speaks of the September afternoon sunlight.

qa.q: How is the laburnum top described at the start?
qa.e: The tree is silent and still before the bird arrives.

qa.q: Which detail shows the season is ending?
qa.e: Yellowing leaves and fallen seeds mark late summer turning to autumn.

qa.q: 'Startlement' means:
